New York Tribune, Aug. 1. Denmark and the Dnehies. lie-commencement of Hostilities. Little doubt exists but that hostilities have ere this, actually commenced between Denmark and the Duchies. It so, important results are likely to ensue, as a large Russian fleet is off the coast, for tiie avowed purpose of giving the Danes all the assistance tiiey may .require. Dates from Hamburg to the 15th, state that a hostile movement on the part of Denmark has been made. 8he had placed her troops across the frontier of the Duchies with the intention, it is said, of enforcing her claim in a decisive manner. Holstein is supported by Brunswick, Hanover and a few of the German Confederated States, w bile Denmark has the firm support of a Russian licet ot about 18. sail of the line. It is reported that the Prussians have made a retrograde movement from Schleswig, and that, the Danish Quartermaster has sent orders on as far as Flensburgh to have quarters prepared for a large body of troops to be placed in occupation. Several of the German and Prussian officers have joined the Holstein army with a view to active service. In addition to the 18 sail of Russians, it is said that additional vessels have been seen off Rostock. The correspondent of the þÿ London þÿHerald says þÿ the greatest anxiety is now manifested to ascertain how far the Russian Government will intervene to put a stop to any further intervention. þÿ The Hanoverian Chamber has expressed the greatest dissatisfaction at the Peace,

and it is likely that the Chamber will force the Government to render all the protection it can to the cause of the Stadtholderate against Denmark in which ease there is much reason to apprehend war, and one in which England will be more or less mixed þÿup. Another correspondent, writing on the evening of the 15th, says, þÿ I have no reasonable question that a couple of battalions of Holstein infantry have entered the Duchy of þÿSchleswig. Intelligence has been received and posted in the Borsenlmllc, to the effect that the head-quarters of the Schleswig Holstein Army were to be, and are this day, in the town of Schleswig. Consequently, the war may be said to have commenced. Six Danish and Russian ships of war have been cruising since yesterday before the harbor of Kiel.

From the Liverpool Albion, August 2G. PROJECT TO OPEN UP TIIE RE- SOURCES OF AFRICA HY A STEAM SHIP LINE.

Our American accounts received by the steam-ship Asia, last week, announced the partial success, in the American House of Representatives, of a project to unite Liberia to the United States by a line of steamships of large tonnage. So unexpected, novel, and striking a scheme is not unworthy, however, of more extended notice than in our last we were enabled to give : and we trust our readers will find in the appended outlines of the Report from the Committee on Naval Affairs a promise of amelioration to Africa of the most important character : Mr. Stanton, of Tennessee, from the Committee on Naval Affairs, to whom was referred the memorial of Joseph Bryan, of Alabama, for himself and his associates, George Nicholas Sanders and others, praying the establishment of a line of steamers from the United States to the Coast of Africa, designed to promote the colonization of free persons of colour, to suppress the African slave trade, to carry the mails, and to extend the commerce of the United States, have made a highly-favourable report on the subject to the House, from which we subjoin the following extracts. After reciting the advantages of this proposed line of steamers, in colonizing free blacks, in suppressing the slave trade, and in opening the rich commercial resources of Africa, such as palm oil, gold dust, ivory, coffee, sugar, dyewood, gums, &.C., the committee speak of the plan as follows: þÿ From the foregoing considerations, the committee believe it to be wise and

politic to accept the proposition of the memorialists, with some modifications which meet with their approval. þÿ Instead of four ships, it is proposed to make the line consist of three, which shall make monthly trips to Liberia, touching on their return at certain points in Spain, Portugal, France, and England. Thus one will leave New York every three months, touching at Norfolk and Charleston for passengers, freight, and mails; and one will leave New Orleans every three months, with liberty to touch at any of the West India Islands. They will proceed directly to Liberia, with liberty to touch at any of the islands or ports on the Coast of Africa; thence to Gibraltar, carrying the Mediterranean mails ; thence to Cadiz, or some other port of Spain, to he designated by the Government; thence to Lisbon ; thence to Rrest, or some other port of France, to be designated as above ; and thence to London, bringing mails from all those points to the United þÿStates. The measure proposed by the committee contains the following stipulations and provisions, to wit : þÿ Each ship to be of not less than 4,000 tons burthen, and the cost of each not to exceed 000,000 dollars. The

ST <S & 1 i?2 3. Government to advance two-thirds of the cost of construction from time to time, as the building progresses, the advance to be made in five per cent, stocks, payable at the end of thirty years, such advances to be repaid by the contractors in equal annual instalments, beginning and ending with the service. The said ships to be built in accordance with plans to be submitted to and approved by the Secretary of the Navy, and to be so constructed as to be convertible, at the least possible expense, into war steamers of the first class. þÿ The ships to be kept up by alterations, repairs, additions, to be approved by or the Secretary of the Navy, so as to be at all times fully equal to the exigencies of the service, and the faithful performance of the contract. þÿ Each ship to be commanded by an officer of the navy, who, with four midshipmen to serve as w atch officers, shall be accommodated in a manner suitable to their rank, without charge to the Government. The Secretary of the Navy at all times to have the right to place on board of each ship two guns of heavy calibre, and the men necessary to serve them to be accommodated and provided for by the contractors. þÿ The Secretary of the Navy to exercise at all times such control o\er the said ships as may not be inconsistent with these terms, and to have the right to take them, or cither of them, in case of war, for the exclusive use and service of the United States, on paying the value thereof, such value, not exceeding the

cost, to be ascertained by appraisers mutually chosen by the Secretary and the contractors. The Secretary also to have the power to direct, at the expense of the Government, such changes in the machinery and the internal arrangements of the said ships, or any of them, as he at any time may deem advisable. þÿ The contractors are further required to stipulate to carry, on each and every voyage they may make, so many emigrants, being free persons of colour, and not exceeding 2,500 for each voyage, as the American Colonization Society may send, the said society paying in advance ten dollars for each emigrant over twelve years of age, and five dollars for each under that age, these sums to include the transportation of baggage, and the daily supply of þÿsailors rations. þÿ The contractors also to convey, free from cost, such necessary agents as the Government or the Colonization Society may require, upon each one of said ships. þÿ Two of said ships to be finished and
and the other within three years after the execution of the contract. þÿ The Government to pay forty thousand dollars for each and every trip, and to exact ample security for the faithful

taking security in the ships for the repayment of the sums advanced. The contract to continue fifteen years from the completion of all the ships. þÿ To assist in forming a correct judgment as to the fairness of this compen-

sation the committee present an estimate of the probable cost of running the said ships. þÿ The cost of the ships, at 900,000 dollars, w ill be 2,700,000 dollars. Upon this amount interest should he calculated at six per cent. ; for, although the contractors will pay the Government but five per cent, on the portion advanced, the balance supplied by the contractors must be estimated at the rates in New York and New Orleans, which are above six per cent. Six per cent, will be a fair average for the whole. þÿ The depreciation of this kind of property is estimated variously, sometimes as high as ten percent, per annum on the total costs ; but, as these ships will be substantially built for war purposes, it may be estimated at a lower rate. þÿ Besid es this, an allowance must be made for repairs. New boilers will be required every six years, and the substitution of these for the old ones not only causes loss ol time, but also injury to the ships, involving much expense. þÿ The rate of insurance for this species of property is high. The committee are informed that the steam-ships Ohio and Georgia pay eight and a half per cent. þÿ Add the expense of running the ships: namely, fuel, wages of the crew, provisions, stores, dock charges, harbour dues, agents, pilotage, lighthouse dues, &c., which cannot be estimated at less than 50,000 dollars per voyage, considering that the distance to Liberia, and then home via Madeira, Gibraltar. Cadiz, Lisbon, Brest, and London, is

about 12,000; and that each voyage, with the necessary delays in the various ports, will occupy about three months þÿ STATEMENT OF EXPENSES. T nl nrpst on 2,700,000, at 6 per cent 102,000 dollar. Depreciation and repairs at 10 per cent 270,000 þÿ Insurance, 7 per cent 180,000 þÿ Cost þÿoi running the ships, 50,000 dollars per voyage, twelve voyages per annum 600,000 þÿ

Tola! annual expense 1,121,000 þÿ , þÿ PROFITS. E-liinaling 1,500 passengers for each voyag and twelve voyages per , annum, we have 18,000 passengers. These, 10 dollars for adults and 5 dollars for children, may average a profit of 3 dollars each, making 54,000 Government pay 480,000 þÿ

Balance of expense over Government pay and profit of emigrants - - 687,000 þÿ þÿ Thus, it will be seen that the conready for sea within two-and-a-half years, more than two thirds of a million, or tractors have of their probable expense, 57,250 dollars each voyage, to be made by commerce and passengers, independent of the Government pay and the profit from the Colonization Society. It is quite evident that any further profit, performance of the contract, besides | beyond the ordinary rate of interest at six per cent., will be contingent upon the success of the enterprise in stimulating commerce with the United States at the points regularly touched at bj these steamers. The contractors have confidence in this, and the committee do

not doubt that their confidence will be rewarded to a reasonable extent. þÿ It will be observed, that, as the Colonization Society now pay for the transportation of emigrants to Liberia in sailing vessels, not less than thirty dollars per head, the proposed arrangement will make the actual cost eventually less than this, even adding the amount to be paid by the United States for this service to the amount to be paid by the said society, without estimating the receipt from mails, which will probably be þÿlarge. LEGAL ADVICE. Rennes, (lie ancient capital of Brittany is a famous place for law. People came there from the extremities of the country to get information and ask advice. To visit Rennes without getting advice appears impossible to a Breton. This was true at the latter end of the last century, just as it is at the present, and especially among the country-people, who are a timid and cautious race. Now it happened one day that a farmer named Bernard, having come to Rennes on business, bethought himself that as he had a few' hours to spare, it would be well to enjoy them in getting the advice of a good lawyer. He had often heard of Monsieur Poticr de lay Germondale, who was in such high repute that people believed a law suit gained when he undertook their cause. The countryman inquired for his address, and proceeded to his house in Rue St. Georges. The clients were numerous, and Bernard had to wait some time. At length his turn arrived, and he was introduced. M. Potier de la Germondale signed to him to be seated, then taking off his spectacles and placing them on his desk, he requested to know his business. þÿ Why, Mr. þÿLawyer, said the farmer, þÿtw irling hat, þÿ his have I heard so much about you, that, as I have come to Rennes, I wish to take the opportunity of consulting þÿyou. þÿ I thank you for your confidence, my friend : you wish to bring an action, perhaps þÿ? þÿ An action! oh, I hold that in abhorrence ! Never has Pierre Bernard had a word with any þÿone.

þÿ Then it is a settlement þÿ a division of property þÿ! þÿ Excuse me, Mr. Lawyer; my family and I have never made a division, seeing that we all draw from the same well, as they þÿsay. þÿ Well, is it to negotiate a purchase or a sale þÿ? þÿ Oh, no! I am neither rich enough to purchase, nor poor enough to sell þÿ! þÿ Will you tell me, then, w hat you do want of þÿme! said the lawyer in surprise þÿ Why, I have already told you, Mr. þÿLawyer, replied Bernard. þÿ I want your advice for payment, of course, as þÿ I am well able to give it to you, and I þÿdon w t ish to loose this þÿopportunity. Mr. Potier took a pen and paper, and asked the countryman his name. þÿ Pierre þÿBernard, replied the latter, quite happy that he was at length understood. þÿ Your age þÿ? þÿ Thirty years, or very near þÿit. þÿ Your vocation þÿ? þÿ My vocation ! Oh, that means what 1 do ? I am a þÿfarmer. The Lawyer wrote two lines, folded the paper, and handed it to his strange client. þÿ Is it finished already? Well and good. What is the price of that advice, Mr. þÿLawyer! þÿ Three francs þÿ!

Bernard paid the money and took his leave, delighted that he had taken advantage of this opportunity. When he reached home it wras four þÿo clock; the journey had fatigued him, and he determined to rest himself the remainder of the day. In the meantime the hay had been two days cut, and was completely saved. One of the workingmen came to ask if it should be drawn in. þÿ What, this þÿevening? exclaimed the þÿfarmer wife, s who had come in to meet her husband. þÿ It would be a pity to commence the work so late, since it can be done to-morrow without any inconveþÿnience. The man objected that the weather might change ; that the horses j were all ready, and the hands idle. But the | þÿfarmer wife s replied that the wind was in good quarter, and that night would set in before their work could be completed. Bernard, who had been listening to the argument, was uncertain which way to decide, when he suddenly recollected | that he had the þÿlawyer s advice in his j pocket. þÿ Wait a þÿminute, he exclaimed; þÿ I have an advice and a famous one too þÿ þÿ that I paid three francs for ; it ought to tell us what to do. Here Theresa, see what it says ; you can read written hand better than þÿI. The woman took the paper, and read this line þÿ þÿ never put off till tomorrow' WHAT YOU CAN 1)0 TO-DAY þÿ! þÿ That þÿit, s exclaimed Bernard, struck with a sudden ray of light. þÿ Come, be quick ; get the carts, and away ; boys and girls, all to the þÿhayfield! His wife ventured a few more objec-

tions, but he declared that he had not bought a three-franc opionion to make no use of it, and that he would follow the þÿlawyer advice. s 11c himself set the example by taking the lead in the work, and not returning till all the hay was brought in. The event seemed to prove the wisdom of his conduct, for the weather changed during the night ; an unexpected storm burst over the valley ; and the next morning it was found that the river had overflowed, and carried away all the hay that had been left in the fields. The crops of the neighboring farmers were completely destroyed; Bernard alone had not suffered. The success of this first experiment gave him such faith in the advice of the lawyer, that from that day forth he adopted it as the rule of his conduct, and became, by his order and diligence, one of the richest farmers in the country. He never forgot the service done him by M. Potiere de la Germondale, to whom he ever afterwards carried a couple of his finest fowls every year as a token of gratitude.
If you wish oaks, plant acorns ; but if you wish a fortune, plant dollars ; but if you prefer happiness, sow the seeds of virtue and þÿ cultivate them with charity.

From the London Illustrated News CHRISTIAN JULIUS DE MEZA, MA- JOR-GENERAL, AND COMMANDER- IN-CHIEF OF THE DANISH ARTIL- LERY.

The French-sounding name of Major- General de Meza, whose promptitude and decision determined the fortunes of the battle of Idstedt, may, perhaps, have led strangers to infer that, though serving in the Danish army, this distin guished oflicer was not born to be a de- ! fender of the country whose cause be has so nobly served. But, happily for she has not in her hour ot trial bad to seek abroad for men capa

Me of loading her brave sons to battle ; and Christian Julius de Meza is a Dane by birth and education. Born followed in Elsinore, where his father in 1792, the profession of a doctor of medicine, be entered, in 1804, the artillery branch of the Royal Military Academy in Copenhagen ; and, in 1807, then only titteen years of age, lie served his apprenticeship in war against the English, who in that year made their memorable attaek upon Copenhagen. In 1811, Lieutenant de Meza was appointed teacher of military geography and Danish history in the military school for artillery cadets, in Copenhagen ; and, in 1813, he was raised to the position of Adjoint on the Staff of the Quarter-Master-General. Owing toareduction which took place, he soon again lost this appointment, and resumed his position in the corps of Artillery and at the Military Academy. In 1821, Captain de Meza married Miss Tscherning (sister of Captain Tscherning, the lirst Minister of War under the new constitutional regime in Denmark,) and in 1825 he commenced a foreign tour, being charged by the Government with examining into and reporting upon the it \teriee of the artillery and the state of the principal military schools in the Rhenish provinces of Germany, as also in Holland, France, Italy, and England. In this county the attainment of Captain de þÿMeza sobject was facilitated by the especial kindness of Lord Fitzroy Somerset. who in spite of the dislike then prevailing to allow foreigners more than a

superficial glance at our establishments at Woolwich wrote to General Ramsay, requesting that be would permit the Danish officer to take small sketches of the various objects which might seem to him to deserve especial notice. Having been equally successful in the other countries which lie had visited, the result of his tour was a mass of valuable notes and drawings, the arranging and copying out of which occupied several years. In 1828, the year after his return home, de Meza advanced to the command of a battery ; and in 1829 he was made a Knight of the Dannehrog. He had already resumed his duties as teacher at the Artillerv Academy ; and when, in 1830, this establishment was superseded by a Military High School, Captain de Meza being distinguished for his knowledge of the languages and literatures of Europe, was appointed professor of both in the new institution. In this position he continued until F47 ; undertaking, however, in the interval, a new journey to Paris, with a view to the publication of a French pronouncing dictionary prepared by him, but which, owing to the disastrous circumstances of the publishing trade in France at that period was not carried out. I p to this moment it had been the faith of Major de Meza to belong to an army for a long period of years not called into active service, and whose efficiency for such an emergency remained untested ; but as an indefatigable man of science he had gained for himself a position among the honoured in his country.

On the breaking out of the war in the Duchies Major de Meza, who had reentered active service in the corps of Artillery was, in March 1848, ordered to take the command of the batteries of Artillery forming part of the North Jutland Army Corps. The artillery force engaged in the campaign of that year was subsequently considerably augmented, and continued until the end of the year under the command of Major de Meza who directed its operations at Ban and Flensburg, as also, at Schleswig, at Wvbel. and at Dyppel. The great skill and gallantry evinced by the commander in these various employments obtained for him the warmest thanks of the Ge-

3®, « 3t 1 Z $> A?13» neral commanding the army and of the Minister of War, who immediately after the affiiir of Dyppel, promoted him to the rank of Lieutenant-Colonel. On the 18th of September, the grateful acknowledgments of his Sovereign were added to those of his superior officer, King Frederick VII. presenting to him with his own hands, after the great review of the army of the north, the silver cross of the Dannehrog, saying, þÿ Wear this in remembrance of þÿme.

In December, 1848, de Meza was promoted to the rank of Colonel, and appointed to the command of the 6th Brigade of Infantry, which assembled at Als in 1849. On the 16th of April of that year, Colonel de Meza having obtained the brevet rank of Major-General, succeeded Major-General von Billow in the command of the three brigades (about 15,000 men) then stationed in the island, as well as of the whole artillery force on the spot. It: this position he abstained with wise moderation from all unnecessary and profitless waste of powder and shot, and remained on the defensive, thus saving the town of Sonderburgh from repeated bombardment, which would inevitably have followed, had he given in to the opinion of those who wished the batteries on the coast to keep up a constant cannonade against the earthworks thrown up by the enemy to protect their position on the opposite shore. Every attempt at an advance on the side of the enemy was, however, instantly and energetically repelled. þÿ According to a secret understanding between de Meza and Major-General Billow, who had assumed the command of the north army corps, the 6th Brigade was, towards the end of June, conveyed over to Fiinen ; and, on the 1st of July, de Meza himself left the island of Als for that of Fiinen, under pretext of inspecting various sea-coasts and ports, but in reality to repair to the quarters of the Commander-in-chief in Fiinen, where the sortie from the fortress of Frederick!, which was afterwards so gloriously

effected, was determined upon. On the memorable night between the 5th and 6th ot July, 1849, Major-General de Meza commanded the vanguard, formed of the 6th Brigade. As lie was issuing from the gates of the fortress at the head of his staff, an aide-de-camp came galloping up to ask if it would not be advisa- i ral attack projected. On hearing this, ble for the soldiers to take their bayonets off their muskets, as the glittering ot the steel in the moonlight might attrack the þÿenemy s attention, and loo early reveal their intentions. þÿ We cannot remove everything that þÿglitters, Subsequently two distinguished officers was the þÿGeneral s reply. þÿ The principal thing is to have the bayonets in readiness at the decisive moment, and that will soon be here ; therefore, leave them þÿon. On the preceding evening the General had, indeed intimated to his troops that, in the coming engagement, they would be called upon to thrust down, rather than shoot down, their enemies, and the men had responded enthusiastically to the intimation. The first assault of the Danish vanguard on the batteries of the besieging army was, in consequence, made bayonet hand, in without a shot being loosened ; and though received by a murderous tire, the 6th Brigade did not quail but went on storming and taking entrenchment after entrenchment until sunrise, when all the works on Igurn road were in the hands of the Danes. In the afternoon, such of the enemy as had not fallen or been made

prisoners were in full flight, and the another horse it received Danes remained undisputed victors on the field of Fredericia þÿ I had given you a difficult task to þÿperform, said the Commander-in-Chicf to Major-General de Meza, when the assembled renerals were congratulating each other

on the success of the day; and the brave officer replied, warmly, thanking his superior for having entrusted him with so honourable a post. During the whole of this sanguinary battle he maintained his position in the centre of his own line; the imperturbable coolness which he evinced, while the balls of the eneþÿmy smusketry and artillery were raining down about him, being only once disturbed by an ebullition of feeling, which did not surprise those acquainted with the vivacity of his temperament and the warmth of his feelings. His favourite horse, which had borne him through all the previous engagements, having received several wounds, he dismounted, and under the melancholy impression that he had lost the faithful animal for ever, he commenced writing a report to the Commander-in-Chief. þÿ \\ hen, therefore, this being concluded, the horse was brought back to him refreshed and strengthened, he was so overcome by emotion that he threw his arms round the neck of the animal, and gave it an affectionate kiss.

Immediately after the battle of Fredericia, de Meza was promoted to the rank of Major-General, and on the 12th of September he was nominated Knight Commander of the order of the Damichrog. On the 1st of January, 1850, he was appointed Commander-in-chief of the Royal Artillery, but having during the winter suffered from a most painful malady, and undergone a dangerous surgical operation, he was unable, at the expiration of the armistice, to accept immediately an active command in the army. As soon, however, as his health permitted it, and he was able again to mount a horse, he repaired to the armv, and held himself disposible. He was thus present, when, on the morning ot the battle of Idstedt (25th July), the general commanding the army, Von Krogh, received intelligence that the brave General Schleppegrell, commanding the second division, was mortal!) wounded, that the greater number of his officers forming his staff were either killed or wounded, that several other officers of rank orof distinguished merit had fallen, and that in consequence a certain degree of confusion reigned in the division, and that it was feared that it would not be able to bear its part in the gene-
General Von Krogh turned to General de Meza, and requested him to repair to the field of action, and see what could be done; and the latter instantly depart ed followed by six ordonances þÿonly.

were despatched to serve as his staff, and one of General þÿScldeppegrell aides- s de-camp, though wounded in the arm, continued during 12 hours to do service. Three-quarters of an hour after his arrival on the field of battle, General de Meza was able to inform tlve Commander-in-Chief that he had succeeded in rallying the division of Schleppegrell, and in gathering a force sufficient to execute the projected movement. He then led the army to the attack, and after some hours of desperate and sanguinary fighting, the battle of Idstedt was won by the Danes. Notwithstanding his chivalrous bravery, General de Meza has escaped unhurt from every engagement in which he has taken part ; but at the battle of Idstedt, the favourite charger, mentioned above, was shot under him, and the servant who brought him two wounds while holding for his master to mount. This faithful attendant, who nursed the General through his late severe illness, did not, however give up his charge, but continued near his master to the end of the battle.

St. Lucia Palladium. The \i h .ludieial Sjslcin. 15 y the Steamer which becomes due to-morrow from Barbados, it is anticipated, Sir Robert Bowcher Clarke will make his first visit to this Island, preparatorily to his assuming office as our Chief Judsre in criminal matters, and Judge of Appeal in civil cases. This preliminary visit seems requisite to obtain for His Honour an insight into the peculiarities of our Franco-Anglo system of jurisprudence, to afford him an opportunity of participating in the work of arranging the plan for future operations, and of observing what defects there may be in the existing system to demand correction according to his ideas. Now, there is no denying the high learning of Sir Bowcher, or his competency for the important mission. The public of St. Lucia are big with anxiety as to the practical results of the arrangement which makes him head of their Judicial Administration ; and the sooner, therefore, the details of the plan are settled upon, the better for all parties þÿ its opponents as well as its approvers. There was a time when almost any change in the composition or constitution of our local courts of law would have been hailed as an improvement ; but that time is >ast: it died in the condign degradation of Judge Reddie. So, now, every change that may be proposed is liable to be very closely examined, ere admitted to be an amelioration. For our part, and we have considered the matter well, we do not see in what way the new system can be recommended as one promising any public advantage. þÿ

Our Criminal Assizes occur, under present rule, three times a year, are presided overby a professional Chief and two Assistant Justices, with a Jury of twelve, and with English law and English procedure. It is not likely that this will be materially improved by the fact of our being made a judicial dependency of the island of Barbados. þÿ And, as to the Civil Court, now composed of a professional Chief Justice and two Assistants, who sit twice a month or oftener, þÿ where is the improvement held forth under the new constitution ? True, it is most desirable to facilitate the means of access to an appellate tribunal, such a tribunal being now þÿ owing to the expense, and delay of recourse to the higher court in England þÿ almost inaccessible to suitors feeling aggrieved here. But to increase the causes for

three local Judges must inevitably do, seems to us anything but an improvement; as, many cases which would have been satisfactorily decided in the course of one month by a bench of three Judges, will now be fettered with additional delay and expense in the constant appeals that will naturally have to be made from awards given by a single Judge, and where those appeals can only be heard every four or six months, as the Barbados Judge (whoever he may be) shall make his periodical visits. Be-

3 3N ®Si»J2 A T 1 S-. sides, we abhor the system altogether which w ould rest the appellate jurisdiction in the hands of any one individual, be that individual a Sir Bowcher Clarke or a Lord Denman. What must these appeals amount to? þÿ one lawyer reversing or approving the judgment of o.m: other lawyer. No one denies the firstrate abilities of Sir Bowcher ; nor do we over-rate the merits of Mr. Atthill (our local Judge under the reformed system) in pronouncing him in nowise inferior to the learned Knight as a lawyer ; þÿ neither do we care which of the two may be the better man. But all things are mutable here below. Is it impossible that a Chief Justice of Barbados should, at some time or other, be less learned, less independent, or less honest in his vocation, than the resident Judge in St. Lucia, whose decisions he might be called upon to review in his appellate capacity ? Then, what monstrous absurdity is not a system so provocative of expense, delay, and vexation to suitors at law, whilst it degrades to the dust a community striving for social improvement and aspiring to institutional advancement! Independently of these considerations, we see many reasons for thinking the system impracticable. Sir Bowcher, we feel sure, will himself soon grow as heartily tired of the work, as the people will lie disgusted with the scheme ; and it will be most satisfactory to behold a return to the system of Circuit Courts as originally projected.

Junction of the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. þÿ The convention between her Majesty and the United States of America, relative to the establishment of a communication by ship canal between the Atlantic and Pacific, was signed at Washington on the 19th of April last, by Sir II. L. Bulwer and Mr. Clayton, secretary of state of the United States, and the ratifications were exchanged on the 4th of July. According to the articles of the convention, the two governments declare that neither the one nor the other will ever obtain any exclusive control over the ship canal, erect any fort ilicat ions commanding the same, or exercise any dominion over Nicaragua, Costa Rica, the Mosquito Coast, or other part of Central America. It is also agreed that vessels of Great Britain and the United States traversing the canal shall, in case of war between the contracting parties, be exempted from blockade, detention, or capture by either of the belligerents; appeal, as the substitution of one for that the persons employed in making the canal shall be protected ; and that, when completed, its neutrality shall be guaranteed, so that it may ever be open and free. It is likewise contracted that the two governments shall give their support and encouragement to all persons who may first offer to commence the undertaking.

This naval force is divided into live squadrons ; the Baltic squadron consists of about 40,000 men, including the artillery ; but the paper states that the crews are not of the very best quality of men, and amongst them are many Jews from þÿPoland.

Premature Interments in Mexico. þÿ Two horrible incidents, which show the danger of premature lntermert, lately took place in the city of Mexico. A woman was attacked by cholera, and apparently died. She was interred in the cemetry of Santa Palma : but just at that moment she awoke from her trance, and, the earth being new ly laid over her. she succeeded in scratching her way out. The other case was that of a woman who, being drunk, was thought dead, and was consequently buried. In a short time the drunkenness passed oil, and she managed to escape from her tomb; but her singular appearance drew around her a perfect crow d of leopards, by whom she was chased home. þÿ New Orleans Picayune.

A IJINNLR. PARTY AT WINDSOR PALACE. For the accuracy of the following we c ut confidently answer ; it may he interesting to those who never saw, and are never likely to see, Majesty eating, drinking, liv ing:, and moving in the interior of ii palace. < 31 an officer of great intelligence, and associated in a work ot uincli interest connected with the ancient Scripture History of India, arrived a short time since in this country, and his arrival, together with some observations oh the work in which he was engaged, ippeared in the London papers. A few lavs after he was surprised to receive at his hotel, through the lord chamberlain, an invitation, or perhaps we should rather call it a command, to dine at the Palace at Windsor þÿ an honour which surprised him, as he was only just arrived from India, and had never been presented at court. He determined of course to comply with the august and agreeable command, and as the invitation intimated he was to come in court dress, or words tantamount to that, he proceeded to a tailor, who fitted him out in the usual adornment befitting him for he high company amongst whom he was about to appear. At the thistle he presented himself on the following day, and was received by the tall magnificent footmen in scarlet liveries, one or two of whom stood on each landing, and silent as mutes, but more gorgeous, pointed their fingers in the direction lie was to take. Following up the grand staircase the course this line of brilliant linger posts pointed out, lie entered one

anti»room, where lie was received by some high officer, and directed to another, and at length found himseli in one where some gentlemen similarly attired as himself were waiting in a group. He had little trouble, as soon as he composed his senses, after the unusual scene through which lie had passed, in perceiving that they, like himself, were invited to dinner ; and lie presently recognised one of them, an eminent historian with whom he had been acquainted. Here they remained conversing for a few minutes, wher. suddenly the folding doors at one end of the room were thrown open, and preceded by the grand chamberlain with his rod of office, her Majesty, leaning on l'rincc Albert, appeared, and without pausing to take cti.t notice of her guests, passed quite through t lie room in which tlicy were, mil out through corresponding doors .vhich led to the dining or banqurttingioom on the other side, the company, amongst whom was M , falling in the rear, and silently following. They took their seats, Prince Albert next to her Majesty, and the other guests down the table, which was not large, as the dinner party was a limited one. There was no general conversation þÿ the guests spoke in subdued lones to each other, her Majesty spoke to none, and the prince only let fall a few words to some one near him, until at length t lie few words gradually grew fewer; this, how-

3 T Q li 0 1 X. AT I 3 ever, was not so awkward as a silent dinner party might seem under other circumstances, as the magnificent hand of the Coldstream Guards in an adjoining apartment were playing the finest i not be executed. airs, and good music is any day better than indifferent conversation. Nevertheless, it was a chilling scene, and as soup, fish, and ilesli wen handed round by the " tall fellows" in crimson, some by llavnau is removed, no doubt thought they would prefer, as a general rule, less grandeur and more cordiality. Dinner concluded, her -Ma- 1 general will decline. declares jesty remained a short time, then arose and again preceded by the officers ot state returned to the drawing-room, as 1 suppose we may call it; never having spoken all the tunc to her company. þÿ The prince's mood, however, became more hearty as soon as her Majesty had left and lie led in a general and lively conversation on antiquarian subjects, in which he displayed large reading and great intelligence. While they were thus pleasantly and intellectually engaged, it was announced that her Majesty expected their presence to coffee, and they proceeded to the drawing-room, where the Queen with her ladies in waiting was. llere matters again relapsed into the same splendid state silence as in the early part ot the dinner. Coll'ee was handed round, and each guest mutely sipped his cup, regarding Majesty, if one might so speak from a distance. While M was wondering when the signal to depart would be given, the graiul chamberlain advanced,

and informed him that her Majesty had given orders that he should be presented ; he therefore cauie forward to where her Majesty was seated in the same room, and with as much form .ts though he had not met her at dinner, he knelt and touched with his lips the hand that was offered, and this ceremony gone through, again retired, lully expecting that this was an end ol a stately but somewhat stupid day. Hut it was not so, for a quarter of an hour subsequently he was informed that her Majesty, who retired to a kind of alcove or recess, about as deep as an embayed window, wished to converse with him; he accordingly presented himseli before his sovereign, w ho, no longer in formal state, immediately entered with vivacity and intelligence into conversation on the particular and interesting, and, in many respects, learned subject in which lie had been engaged, showing in all her inquiries and observations a well-stored, clear, and cultivated mind. When her Majesty had conversed for some time, and sufficiently informed herself, she rose, and Mr. retired, and soon after he and the other guests departed.' This to us appears strange ; but if her Majesty bad not the prerogative of speaking, and being spoken to only when she wished, the multitude <>t her company and receptions would be laborious and wearisome þÿ Bristoi Times.

The American ship "Nebraska," 525 tons, Captain Toone, came to an anchor in our port on Monday morning 6 a. m. in a leaky state. The Nebraska sailed from the port of Shanghae, Canton, ori the evening of Friday t he 29th March last (out 157 days to this port) hound to New York, laden with a valuable cargo of Silks and Tea. After being out eighty days she experienced very heavy weather off the Cape of Good Hope, which continued with such intense severity for a period of twenty-eight days, that the Captain on many occasions, despaired ever making the land; during the continuance of this weather the ship sprung aleak, which increased considerably her perilous situation. On the 14th of July the gale abated, and the Captain proceeded to put the ship in such trim s . circumstances allowed, and shaped Lis course for St. Helena, where he arrived on the 1st of August. Finding that port already filled with distressed shipping and supplies at incalculable high prices, he resolved to proceed on his home voyage and consequently left the port on the morning of the 3rd. A second gale of less severity was experienced the second week out, which increased the leak to so alarming an extent, that the Pumps have not ceased to work since that time, for even an intermission of five minutes. Captain Toone lias consigned his ship to Messrs. J. B. Vnduze A Sons, and has commenced to discharge her cargo, and will possibly when empty, be taken on our Marine Slip to undergo repairs.

This document occupies more tha five columns of the Diaro i>e i.a M arena We lay before our readers a brief bu comprehensive analysis of it. The Auditor sets out by alledgingtli law, and the authority under which tb vessels and persons on board of then have been captured, and are detaine and tried. The General Marine Ord nances of Spain of 1793 are referred to. lie then notices the attempt made las year to invade Cuba. The expeditio was got up by some Cuban refugees, ri siding in the United States, assisted b speculators. " Among the elements nr cessary for such an enterprise they relie upon a portion of the adventurers wlu

in the recent war of tlie United States with Mexico, had tasted the sweets of a campaign which, without peril or labor, had procured them well-known advantages," &c. A journal was established in New York to prepare the public mind and to make proselytes. The expedition matured, and was 011 the point of sailing, when, on the 11th of August, 184!), the President published his proclamation, and gave orders to the Navy to force the Round Islanders to disperse. Preparations for a second expedition Were soon commenced, " with more experience and more caution," and the means of fitting it out were procured by the sale of bonds, and of the property of the Island, which was disposed of at public auction. Five hundred and fifty men left New Orleans in three different vessels, and landed at Gardenas, "which became the theatre of crimes known <0 all. It is notorious that a few hours afterwards the Expeditionists were obliged to re-embark, having been routed by a small force, which at the first notice hastened to meet them." This act, says the Auditor, brought forth a universal cry of indignation throughout the " faithful Antilles," which found an echo in France and England. He then sums up the facts resulting from the examination of the witnesses and documents in the cause. The Georgian a left New Orleans on the '25th of April, for Chagres, with provisions and passengers, arrived at the Balize on the 27th, and there received on hoard arms and munitions. She then went to sea, arrived in nine or ten days

at Contoy, where her passengers were landed and drilled for a short time. þÿ They again embarked, and taking a pilot from a fishing smack, were endeavouring to make the Is'and of iMugeres, when lliey were overtaken by the Cnr.oi.r. with an unknown banner, which they designated as the Cuban banner. The Susan Loud left New Orleans on the 2d of May, and transferred her passengers, while at sea, 011 board of the Creole, which left New Orleans on the 5th of the same month, and overtook her on the 7th or 8th. The Creole had 144 passengers on hoard when she left New Orleans, and took in arms, munitions and provision at the Balizc. þÿ When the passengers of the Susan Lot i> were on hoard of the Creole, Colonel Hi nce made a speech to them, in which he explained the object of the expedition, and promised them, in the name of Gen. Loi-ez, eight dollars a day during the war, and four thousand dollars bounty at the end of the war. There were fifty two persons on hoard of the Susan Loud and the Georgiana when they were captured. A. 11. Moore alone confessed that he knew, when he left New Orleans, that he was going to Cuba þÿ that Gen. Quitman was to follow with reinforcements, Ac. The others assert that they thought they were going to Chagres, and thence to California. From the papers found in the desk of Capt. Pendleton, of the Susan Loud, it

ST, AT IS, appears that there were in New Orleans, and at various other points, adventurers affiliated together to invade Cuba. It also appears from these papers, that the soldiers of the expedition were to receive a monthly pay of eight dollars, and from one to four thousand dollars a year ; and the officers from nineteen to twenty thousand dollars, besides the ordinary pay allowed to officers of a corresponding rank in the United States Army. There are also testaments in which they dispose of the property which they expected to receive. There is also a commission sent by A. Ilisell, to one J. Herbert, to raise a squadron of cavalry. A biographical sketch of Gen. Lopez was also found in the desk of Capt. Pendleton. This sketch, says the auditor, is a tissue of inventions, intended to exalt Gen Lopez, and to represent him as the man chosen by the people of Cuba to liberate them from the dominion of Spain. The Auditor then alludes to the conspiracy of Gen. Lopez about the middle of 1848, to his condemnation, arid to his escape from the Island. Gen. Quitman, Judge Smith, Mr. Henderson, Mr. Sigur, Mr. O'Sulivan, Cols. O'Hara anil Pickett are, as it appears from original documents in the record, the main supporters of this expedition. "It is wonderful," exclaims the Auditor, " that men of this sort should find a civilized country, in the streets of which they can walk with their heads erect, and in stations and offices which none even suspected of such crimes would be allowed to retain in any other civilized

country." The Auditor again refers to the landing at Cardenas, to the crimes, excesses, robberies, Ac., committed there, and winds up by informing the world that the expedition has been denounced by the unanimous voice of the press in this country and in Europe with the exception of the Sun and the Delta, and a few others. þÿ It has been qualified as an act of piracy, in the House of Lords, in England, and by the President of the United States; for such he must have considered the Round Islanders when, in his Proclamation, he informed them they should not look to the interference of the United States in whatever extremities they might find themselves. Gen. Lopez is a pirate ; but a pirate of a new species. A pirate who sets up political pretexts, aspires at fame, has presses to defend him, associates, Generals and Judges in his plans and in his robberies. þÿ England, France, Denmark and Sweden, are all interested on account of their possessions in the Atlantic, in punishing this new species of piracy invented by the neighboring Republic. The maritime tribunals have jurisdiction over the whole subject, according to the existing laws and ordinances of Spain. There is ample evidence against the vessels. They were employed in transporting men, arms and munitions, to attack the Island of Cuba, as the subsequent landing of Lopez at Cardenas

has shown. For, all hough they did not go directly to Cuba, they communicated with the Creole, and transferred men, provisions, arms and ammunitions on board of her. Above all, it appears that the papers of these vessels were not. in order, and the Georgiana had no license to take arms on board at the Balize. þÿ For all these reasons the vessels are declared confiscated for the benefit of the State, to be sold or otherwise disposed of. The forty-two passengers found on board of the Susan Loud and the Georgiana, are ordered to he released. For, although the auditor lias sufficient evidence to produce a moral conviction upon his mind, that these men could not have left New Orleans without knowing the real object of the voyage, yet no positive proof of the fact has been obtained. A. B. Moore, alone, confessed openly his knowledge of, and participation in, the enterprise. But he is pardoned at the special request of Armero. The auditor suggests that it would not he proper to allow the liberated prisoners to walk about the streets, or to select the vessel to return to the United. States. The Captain of the Susan Loud and the three sailors who went to Cardenas 011 hoard of the Creole, have been declared ootlaws, by the proclamation of the Captain-General, dated the li)th of May. It will therefore be necessary that the description of these individuals, as it appears from their shipping papers, shall be furnished to the Captain-General, that the law may be executed if thev are

Great interest was excited in Paris on Sunday, by the announcement that M. Poitevcn, an aeronaut, would ascend on

horseback with a balloon on that day. Upwards of 10,000 persons paid for admission to the Champ do Mars to witness the ascent, and outside, on the heights of Chaillot, &c., more than 150,000 individuals were collected. The President of the Republic was present, and was received with great enthusiasm. The balloon was 15 metres in diameter, 47 in circumference, and 20 high, but it only weighed 150 kilogrammes. It was a matter of considerable difficulty to fill the balloon with gas, owing to the violent wind which prevailed, and when it was filled, it was beaten to and fro by the wind so strongly, that several of the spectators had to assist in holding it. At a little before six o'clock, the horse, a handsome dapple grey, was brought out ; a stout cloth was placed round the body of the horse, and several straps, passed over the shoulders and loins, were united in rings, and by these rings the animal was attached by cords to the net-work oi the balloon. A platform ot basket-work, seven or eight feet above the horse, contained the ballast, and to this platform the aeronaut had access by means of a rope-ladder. A cord passing through an opening in the platform, enabled him to open the valve of the balloon. The aeronaut was dressed as a jockey, and had with him several bottles ot wine and some bread. Some confusion was caused by the crowd attempting to force their way into the reserved place, but they were kept off by the soldiers. At length, at ten minutes past six, the horse was

duly attached to the balloon, and M. Poiteven having mounted its back, the signal to rise was given. The horse plunged a little as it lost its footing, but when fairly lifted from the earth it dropped its legs, as is the case when horses are slung for embarkation on shipboard. The balloon rose majestically over the EcoleMilitaire ; but at times the wind was so violent as to drive it in such a position, that it appeared on a level with the aeronaut. The emotion of the spectators was very great, and one lady fainted. M. Poiteven displayed extraordinary sang froid, and saluted with his cap and whip. After a while, he was seen to leave his saddle, and ascend by means of the rope-ladder to the platform containing the ballast, in order to throw some of it away, so as to rise higher. This done, he descended, and again mounted the horse. There was no network or anything to protect him or the animal. The balloon went in the direction of Fontainebleau, and M. Poiteven intended to remain in the air about an hour. The following details are from the aeronant's own account of his ascent : " I had much difficulty in moderating the too great ascensional power, which, in a few minutes, carried me to too great a height, for the horse. There was a copious flow of blood from his mouth. I passed through several counter-currents, which produced an almost constant rotatory movement. I found the cold almost insupportable. When clear of the clouds, I saw some splendid rainbows, and other

3 © 3i 2 A phenomena of the solar rays. About seven o'clock I made preparations for descending, and in three-cpiarters ot an hour after my grapplers were on the ground, but they did not take hold. 1 proceeded in this way for more than a league, when I arrived at the wood of Villemain, near the forest of La Lachelle, commune of Grisi, canton of llrie-Counte Robert (Seine-et-Marne.) During this time my horse, was close to the fields, and bit off the tops of the corn as he passed over it ; and when passing over the high trees he cropped off their leaves. At length 1 was fortunate enough to put an end to this dangerous state of things. Seeing myself near the edge of a dry pond, I vigorously laid hold of a branch of a tree which grew near it, and for an instant checked thecourse of the balloon, and assistance being at hand, 4'J men laid hold of the ropes and it was safely secured. The balloon Was emptied, and the only thing to be regretted is some slight injury to it, from coming in contact with the trees." M. Poiteven was heartily welcomed by the people ; at Grisi he was hospitably received; and at 11 o'clock he left for Paris. þÿ Illustrated London News, July 13.

This young lady has come to this country \\ ith an exhibition ot a very singular and unique character, which has already received the patronage and the express approbation of some of the chief nobility and leaders of fashion. þÿ She has applied herself from an early age to the training of birds ; and the result is, that she exercises over them an extraordinary power, inducing them to perform feats of a wholly different kind from those which have been done by trained animals before. They are, or at least seem to be, acts of intelligence; we say seem to be, because, after the most careful and minute observation, we have been unable to arrive at even a guess as to the manner in which Mdlle. Vandermeersch communicates with the birds. The performance is very simple, and wholly distinct from conjuring or any pretence of" it. The birds are in a cage with several compartments. In front ot the cage is arranged a platform filled with cards, each exactly similar to the other on the side presented to the birds, but bearing various inscriptions on their prefaces, such as the letters of the alphabet, the numerals singly and in combination, the days of" the week, month, or year, the months, the seasons, A c. On the bidding of any one of the comþÿ pany, the birds tell the day ol the week, month, or year ; the seasons; the time by anyone's watch; or they will spell any word indicated, provided it do not contain any one letter twice over. All these things are done with the most
perfect precision, and there is no apparent collusion. Mdlle. Vandermeersch docs not touch the birds or the cards, and the little animals hop out of their cages and pick out the cards with their

X 3% beaks, seemingly with a very serious effort at recollection and calculation. The exhibition excites admiration and surprise wherever it is seen. At present it is confined to the parties of the nobility and gentry; but we had an opportunity of seeing it, on Wednesday last, at the residence of Mdlle. Vandermeersch, No. 2, Baker-street, Portmansquare. It has been witnessed by the Duchess of Sutherland, the Duke of Wellington, the Marquis and Marchioness of Ely, the Marquis and Marchioþÿ ness of Londonderry, the Duke and Duchess of Bedford, and many other of the principal nobility. Mdlle. Yendermeersch is a native of Toulouse, and is not more than 17 or 18 years of age þÿ a fact which makes her power over these birds the more remarkable. þÿ lb.

ST. CROIX AVIS. Christiansted, September 19, 1850. The Sugar Estates Diamond Ruby, St. Georges, Sally's Fancy and Hope, belonging to the Treasury, were, as previously advertised, put up on Saturday last the 14th instant for lease by public auction, at Government House. The estates are in a high state of þÿcultivation they consist of 405 acres of land in sugar canes, besides 345 acres uncultivated ; and the works, houses for the labourers, and stock arc in proper order. The sale was more than usually attended, and the estates Diamond Sp Ruby were first put up. St. Georges, Sally's Fancy and Hope were subsequently put up, and these were, jointly with Diamond dr Ruby, knocked down to the former renter, His Excellency Governor von Oxhohn, for a term of seven years at $ 10,750 per annum, which amount has exceeded the rate of rent, stipulated bv the Home Government. This is a convincing proof that Sugar Estates here are of some value, although the depressed state of things, it would appear, should tend more to damp the spirit and enterprise of our planters, than to encourage thein on to persevere in the cultivation of the cane. We rejoice to see also that the importation of steam mills and other agricultural implements is daily on the increase, and bids well, we are sure, for the future prospects of the island.

It resulting from the preceding laws respecting the Custom Houses, that the Tariffs approved of by Her Majesty under date of 2nd August, 1849, are more advantageous to the commerce and agriculture of the Island, than those of 1835 w hich are at present in force, with only some slight alterations in the valuation, which will not destroy in its essence the Will of the Supreme Government, in accordance with the opinion of the Junta de Arancclcs and of the superior Dircctiva de Hacienda, I have determined in conjunction with His Excellency the Governor and Captain General on the following : þÿ First. From the 1st of October next, the Tariffs of duties approved of by 11. 31. under date 2nd August, 1849, shall be enforced. Second. As seme articles are not represented at their true value, there being many more of greater value than as appraised, than of those over valued, the alterations indicated in note No. 1 shall be made. Third. The duty of 6£ pr. cent on home productions by national vessels, will be raised to 10 pr. cent, and those of 11£ to 14J l.y foreign vessels to 15 and 18. Those of 23J and 29 on foreign productions by foreign vessels, will be raised to 25 and 30. Those of 15 and 19A to 16 and 20, including weighmoncy, and all others referred to in note 3 of the tariffs. Fourth. All kinds of Jewelry of Gold, Silver, and precious stones of Spanish export shall pay 2 per cent. The same of foreign production per foreign vessel 4 per

cent, and per national vessel 3 per cent. I'ilth. a The barrel of Spanish flour imported per national vessel shall pay for sole duty 3 dollars. The same per foreign vessel 5 dollars. Foreign Hour imported in foreign vessels 7, and in national vessels 5 dollars. Sixth. Virginia leaf tobacco shall pay a fixed duty of 4dollarsper quintal ; Chewing tobacco of like description 5 dollars per quintal, Andullo or long roll foreign, 87 per quintal. Foreign segars 2 dollars per 1000; St. Domingo tobacco (leaf) 5 dollars per quintal ; Cuba leaf 3 dollars per quintal ; Cuba segars 2 dollars per 1000, and each 100 packs of cigarillos of the same class 1 dollar. Seventh. Foreign refined white sugar, in loaf, broken or crushed, shall pay a fixed duty of 8 dollars per quintal, the same from the Is-

land of Cuba 4 dollars, foreign white sugar shall pay 4 dollars per quintal, that of Cuba 2 dollars. Eighth. In addition to the articles declared free of import duty shall also be: ploughs of all kinds, Stills, Trees for cultivation, woodhoops for casks, hoes of every kind, Bristol Temperlime, Iron sluices for Sugar Mills, loose staves of all kinds, furnace bars from any place, fire bricks for furnaces; all machinery for agriculture and irrigation, plants and seeds, plough socks, manure, scientific machinery and apparatus. Ninth. All produce of the country, with the exception of wood, shall be free of royal and municipal duty on exportation. Tenth. Articles arriving from the place of their production shall have a five of benefit in the duty, provided that the merchant obliges himself to export a full cargo of the produce of the country in the vessel which brought the same. Eleventh. From the 1st of October next, when the tariffs will be put in force, articles arriving from non producing ports shall suffer 5 per cent extra duty, another o per cent in 6 months, and another 5 per cent in a year. Twelfth. The tax for the sinking fund being included in the ltoyal duty, vessels which enter in ballast shall be free from that w liich is now charged. Thirteenth. The vessel which only brings cargo for deposit, shall not be liable for tonnage money, provided that the cargo is not introduced for consumption. If 1 lie whole of the cargo should he introduced for consumption, the importer shall pay in addition to

the Custom House duties, the full amount of tonnage and an- < borage dues of the vessel which brought the same, and if only a part of the cargo is brought in for consumption, the tonnage money shall he collected in proportion to its importance. The original says Compuertas de hierro para injenios. THE WASHINGTON NATIONAL MONUMENT, AT WASHINGTON CITY. This grand memorial originated as follows: þÿ In 1763, Congress passed a resolution to erect an equestrian statue to Washington, in the national capital, wherever that should he permanently located. The capital was afterwards

established on the border of the broad and beautiful Potomac, and very appropriately called " Washington City." In 1804, after Washington's death, the subject of a monument to his memory was again broached, but no steps were taken on the matter. In 1833, the " Washington National Monument Society" was organized, with Chief Justice Marshall at its head ; and measures were at once taken to collect the necessary funds. In order that it might truly be a national work, and that the humblest individual could contribute his share, the subscriptions were limited to a dollar. During several years only some thirty thousand dollars were obtained; the hard times of 1837 succeeded, when the entire pecuniary resources of the country were prostrated, and this majestic project seemed hopeless for a time. But, in 1847, new measures were taken, new men and leaders arose ; the collections were increased until they reached eighty thousand dollars ; and the corner-stone was laid, with imposing ceremonies, by the lion. Speaker Winthorp, on the 4th July, 1848. The plan adopted is one worthy of the object. The chief idea in the structure is an obelisk, fifty-five feet square at the base, and intended to be six hundred feet high ! This will exceed, in its alt itude any steeple or monument in the world. From a thickness of fifteen feet the walls diminish to thirty inches, leaving an open space of twenty-five feet square. The top of this noble monument is to be reached by llights of iron

steps at the four sides; and the handrail, being hollow, will serve as a conductor of gas, so that the whole of this prodigious cavern will be rendered as light as day. As to the circular structure þÿ which (to say nothing of its mixed and incongruous architecture) gives such a mufllcd-up appearance to the base þÿ it will he 100 feet high, on a platform 300 feet square. This is intended to serve as the mausoleum of the illustrious dead. The States all contribute a block of stone or marble, and of the kind peculiar to each State. The territory of Mimasota, although scarcely five years have elapsed since the enterprising Yankee commenced to fell her forests, and drive still further back the savage, has sent in her contribution, viz., a slab of the pipestone, used by the Indian exclu-

this is a rare and valuable addition. þÿ Michigan sends a block of pure native copper from her mines in Lake Superior ; and it has been suggested that California should give in one of gold quartz as a specimen of her mountains, which are said to be composed entirely of that material. The little state of Delaware is not a whit behind her younger and overgrown sisters, and sends a block on which she has placed a medallion head of Washington, with this inscription : " Delaware, the first to adopt the constitution, will be the last to abandon it." Tennessee, Missouri, Arkansas, Ohio,

Maine, Massachusetts, have each their contribution in the ground, and with appropriate inscriptions. This desire to pay honour to the father of his country is universal, and has extended even to the Indian. The Chocktaw nation, from their far-off home, are preparing a stone with suitable inscription ; and the Chickasaws have evinced their love for "their great father," by a donation of some two hundred dollars. The sum will be expended in preparing a stone, with simply the motto, "The Chickasaws to their friend."

These stones will be placed in conspicuous positions at the landings of the stairs, and will make a decoration as unique as beautiful. The work is rapidly progressing, and funds are coming steadily in. Agents are canvassing the country in every direction. We have recently seen, in the exciting scenes in Congress, o a ' where the dissolution of the Union was openly avowed, the mere mention of the name of Washington silence the reckless Ultraist, and turn the storm into a calm. There are some persons, and who are admitted to be possessed of both taste and knowledge in architecture, who disapprove of the plan, and say that the old Egyptian massy work, of 100 feet altitude, should support a shaft that resembled something else than an immense chimney or stack to an American factory. But (says our Correspondent) we arc disposed to be pleased, and certainly consider the plan truly an American one, and are sure that no other country will claim it. No country has ever presented a similar spectacle, where all classes so unceasingly united to do honour to one man. Masons and anti-Masons, Old Fellows, benevolent associations, schools, colleges, banks, corporations, have all joined in aiding this project ; and it will truly be a national work, and worthy of the American people. þÿ Illustrated News.

Neglecting the Antecedent. þÿ Some very whimsical instances of this occur continually, especially in the answers of witnesses when given literally as they speak. In a late assault case the prosecutor swore that " the prisoner struck him with a broom on his head till lie broke the top of it !" In narrating an sively for the pipe of peace or war ; accident some time since, it was stated that a poor old woman was run over by a cart aged sixty. So in a case of supposed poisoning: "He had something in a blue paper in his hand, and I saw him put his head over the pot, and put it in !" Another swallowing a base coin: "He snatched the half-crown from the boy, which he swallowed ;" which seems to mean the boy, not the money. An old fellow, who for many years sold combustible matches in London, had the þÿ following cry : " Buy a pennyworth of matches of a poor old man made of foreign wood!" þÿ New York Ciiristmah Bell.

O.n IIl'man Respects. Human Respects are a base disposition of the soul, which makes it act contrary to the lights of its conscience ; an unbecoming weakness, which hinders it from practising good, and induces it to do evil, through fear of displeasing or with a view of pleasing men ; an unworthy complaisance, that engages it to betray its own natural sentiments, which it condemns : a servile depcndance on, and cringing to the opinions of other men, through a desire of acquiring their esteem, or from an apprehension of incurring their censure. According to this definition of human respects, we must not only say, that they degrade human reason, but that they are ihc ignominy and disgrace of religion ; since they reduce Christians to a slavery, which is equally shameful, whether we consider it in itself, in its principle, in its object, or in its universality. The slavery occasioned by human respects is shameful in itself. What more servile, and consequently what more shameful, than to make ourselves dependent on and the slaves of others ; only to regulate our intentions and actions by the intentions and actions of others ; to think, speak, judge, not according to our own lights antl views, but according to the lights and views, let us say mote properly, according to the fancies and capricious humours of others ; to approve of doing good, and not dare to do it ; to condemn evil and let ourselves be drawn into it; to see our obligations, and not have resolution to com-
ply with them ; hardly to have of ourscl\cs either a thought, light, reason, sentiment, or liberty : or else only to have light to run into darkness, reason to give it up, sentiments to degrade

3 To © it % a st AT a a. them, liberty to sacrifice it ? If there are slaves on earth, are there any more base and contemptible than these 1 The slavery of human respects is shameful in its principle : for from what do human respects proceed, but from an unworthy weakness of mind, or from a more unworthy baseness of heart V Ah ! if we possessed that firmness of soul, that nobleness of sentiment, which reason, and much more religion inspires, should we be guilty of such excesses of Weakness and cowardice, and when the world would enslave and tyrannize over us, should we not cry out with the noble generosity of the Apostle : " With me, it is a very small thing to be judged by you ?" Unjust world, what does it import, whether thou accuses orjustifiest me? It is not at thy tribunal, that 1 am to be judged ; it is from the sovereign Judge that 1 expect the equity of my sentence. Thou art often guided by prejudices, fancy, error, illusion ; thy balance is deceitful ; never shalt thou model my sentiments, nor be the regulator of my conduct. Thus would a free mind, and a soul, which feels its own greatness, think and speak ; and in thinking and speaking thus, it would even command the esteem and respect of the world; for the world, depraved as it is, still knows what to think of such persons. But what opinion does it form of and with what eye does it regard those weak men, who neither belong to God nor the world, those double-hearted Christians, those ambiguous soldiers, who are ready to join any part ? They

are not only condemned, but even detested by the world itself. Again, the object of human respects renders our slavery most shameful. There arc certain things, in which we may laudably yield ; there are certain points, wherein, through condescension and deference, we may give up something to others, and put ourselves to some inconvenience. I say still further, slavery itself in some light is tolerable, and even in some just and commendable. But in what concerns religion, faith, conscience, salvation, that is, in things, in which it is necessary to preserve our freedom, and where God himself respects our liberty, to yield and give up our right, is vilifying our character, and carrying shame and ignominy to its greatest height. Let a certain indulgence be used, where things are susceptible of temperament, we may and oftentimes ought to use it ; but to allow ourselves to be ruled in essential points, to be subject in things, which are not susceptible subjection, of to depend in matters, which are most inimical to dependency, is sacrificing, 1 do not say | our liberty, but reason and the very feelings of humanity itself. Finally, the slavery induced by human respects is shameful on account of its universality. For to whom at length n do we become subject ? Of how many persons do human respects make us the unhappy slaves ? Other slaves usually have but one master : let him be unjust, cruel, tyrannical, they have but one ;

whereas the slaves of human respects have as many masters as there are persons, whose discourses they fear, whose approbation they seek, whose censure they dread. Still farther; they have not only as many masters as there are persons, of whom they stand in awe, but as many as these persons themselves have passions. For from the moment a man seeks to content others, he must carefully study all their dispositions, he must become dependent on them ; he must be their slave and the slave of their humours, even to the most abject degree. lie is no longer master of himself ; he dissembles, he betrays his own sentiments, he affects to have the sentiments of others, he dares not appear what he is, and would seem to be what he is not ; he even trembles before those, whose favour lie courts, and stands, as it were, stupified in their presence. Let us at length free ourselves from so great a slavery, let us burst our chains asunder, and shake off our fetters. Being children of God, let us set ourselves at liberty from the slavery of men ; too long we have groaned under the tyranny of human respects ; let us observe the law of God with that holy freedom, which religion inspires. \\ hat are men, and what can they do for us > When we shall be cited to the tribunal of God, will men be able to shelter us from the rigour of his inexorable justice 1 Let us ever remember that we are only accountable to God for our conscience. Little will it import, w hat the judgments of men are, if God stands our friend.
