ST. CROIX AVIS. Christiansted, September 23, 1850. tl'ITOllE OF NEWS. Denmark mid the Duchies. The Hamburgh papers stnte that on the 18th a skirmish took place midway between Schleswig and Rendsburg, between the 10th Holstein battalion, having its position on the outpost of the llolstein army, and advancing northwards, and tire Danish outposts. Tontiing and Frederickstadt are still held by the Danes. Eyderstedt advices report that that district was occupied by the Danes on the 17th instant. A telegraphic despatch from Rendsburg, of the 20th inst., in the Cologne Gazette, states that the entrenchments of that city are now completed, and that the whole of the Ilolstein army left Rendsburg on the 19th, and advanced in the direction of the Danish position. An engagement took place on the evening of the 16th between a Danish steamer, accompanied by two gun-boats, and a Holstein steamer (the Lowe), which was likewise supported by two gun-boats. The combat continued throughout the night. The Lowe has suffered from the enemy's tire, and one of the gun-boats was in danger of being burnt. The Austrian Minister in London has announced the adhesion of his court to the protocol of the 2nd August between Great Britain, France, Russia and Denmark, with a view to a settlement of the Danish question. Austria, as might have naturally been expected, stipulates for the preservation of the rights of the Duchies of Holstein .and Lauenburg, as members of the German Confederation, as well as the rights of the Confederation in relation to the Duchies. To this

there could be, of course, no objection, for there existed no desire for a single moment on the part of the other Powers to interfere with the rights in question, which were, in fact, expressly guarded in the protocol of the 2nd of August. The Berlin journals state that the Danish army could not undertake the attack upon Rendsburgh, and were consequently preparing for their winter quarters in the town and vicinity of Schleswig, and that the Danes were building bridges over the Schley, and erecting for each a strong bridge head. Copenhagen, August 21. The Rus- þÿ sian admiral who commands the fleet in the Baltic has given notice to the lieutenancy-general, that any vessels, bearing either the German flag or that of the duchies, which shall venture into the open sea, shall be treated as pirates by the Russian vessels which shall encounter them. The Gazette de Cologne, of the 26th, says þÿ " According to our advices the Prussian Minister for Foreign Affairs has energetically rejected a proposition contained in a note addressed to him by Lord Palmerston, that he should urge the Schleswig-Ilolstein army to lay down their arms."

i t a Rendsburg, August 22. þÿ Until within the last few days the sanitary condition of the army and of Rendsburg has been all that could be wished. Unhappily a change has suddenly taken place, which is frightening the timid minds among the civil and military classes. The cholera has made its appearance. Ten or twelve fatal of them cases being have an already officer of occurred high rank ; one - Colonel Lessen. The following is General Willisen's report on the losses sustained at the battle of Idstedt : þÿ After a revision of the lists of killed and wounded, prepared by order of the commander-in-chief, on the basis of the hospital reports here, and the communications from Copenhagen and Schleswig, the following results concerning the entire loss of the Schleswig-Holstein army at the battle of Idstedt have been obtained þÿ killed 22 officers, 2 surgeons, 36 sub-ofticers, 476 privates ; wounded (now in this hospital), 31 officers, 73 sub-officers, 687 privates; wonnded, and now in Danish hospitals, 14 officers, 51 sub-officers, 346 privates ; prisoners, 10 officers, 18 surgeons, 57 sub-oiiicers, 1005 privates. Total loss þÿ Officers, 77 ; surgeons, 20 ; sub-officers, 217; privates, 2514. The missing, concerning whom nothing could be further ascertained, are included amongst the fallen. A considerable number of the wounded have left the hospitals, and are now under their colours. The 18 imprisoned surgeons remain voluntarily in the city of Schleswig in charge of the wounded in the

hospitals there. A telegraphic despatch from Hamburgh, in the Cologne Gazette, states that in the evening ol the 26th ult., five Danish vessels approached the Holstein coast near Noerr, and that they effected a landing at Grunewald. Copenhagen letters of the 24th ult., announce the arrival there of the Russian Grand Duke Constantine, who was received by the King of Denmark. Death of llic Ex-liing Louis Philippe. His Majesty King Louis Philippe died on Monday morning, the 26th ot August, at Claremont. The King had been made aware of his approaching dissolution early on the preceding day, in the presence of the Queen, and, receiving with calmness the melancholy information thus first broken to him, prepared for the final arrangements which he wished to make. After a conversation with the Queen, he dictated with a remarkable clearness of mind a conclusion to his memoirs, in order to complete history a which illness had compelled him to suspend for more than four months. 11c then caused to be summoned his chaplain, the Abbe Guellc, all his children and grandchildren who were at Claremont at the time, and in the presence of the Queen and his family he discharged every duty of religion with the most perfect Christian resignation, a stoical firmness, and a simplicity which

is the real evidence of human greatness. He then remained for some time surrounded by his family. Towards seven o'clock in the evening the debility from which the King had been suffering appeared to have passed over, and fever came on, which continued during the night with much violence, but without disturbing the composure of mind, þÿ which never abandoned his Majesty. He expired at 8 o'clock on Monday morning, in the presence of the Queen and the following members of his family : þÿ Their Royal Highnesses the Duchess of Orleans, the Count de Paris, the Duke de Chartres, the Duke and Duchess de Nemours, the Prince and Princess de Joinville, the Duke and Duchess d'Aumale, the Duchess Augusta of Saxe Coburg, and the attached attendants of the royal household.

New York Courier A Enquirer. Important from ltrar.il. We have received by the bark E. Corning, our files of the Jornal de Comercio, published at Rio Janeiro to 7th July, inclusive. We learn from Captain Lloyd, of the bark above named, that there was a great excitement at Rio when he sailed, on the 9th of July, in consequence of the British Steamer Cormorant having taken several Bra/.illian vessels, on suscipion of being slavers, and burnt them in the harbor of Pnranagua. The "Jornal de Comercio," of the 7th July, gives the following account of the affair : "It appears that the "Cormorant" was coming into the port with the four captured Bra/.illian barks þÿ the names of of which arc the " Lconidas, Astrcn, Serca and Anna" þÿ when the commander of the Brazillian fort opened afire upon the " Cormorant," and killed one of the British sailors. The "Cormorant," after responding to the fire, went out and burnt the four captured barks. " The version of this affair is very incomplete," says the Jornal, " but it appears the English Admiral acted under orders received from his government for the suppression of the slave trade." The tw o Houses of Congress arc yet in session, and engaged in the discussion of local matters. The sickness had greatly abated at Rio Janeiro when the bark " E. Corning" sailed from that port.

MAGNETISM IN PAKIS. Four persons were tried on Thursday week by the Tribunal of Correctional Police of Paris on charges of swindling, illegal exercise of medicine, fortune telling, and explanation of dreams. They consisted of a woman named Montgruel, calling herself " La Sybille Moderne," the somnambulist; of her husband, who assisted her in her business ; of a Polish physician named Grabowski, who signed her prescriptions ; and of a Polish druggist, named Sokolowski, who made up the physic. Montgruel had, it appeared, been a primary schoolmaster, and had allowed his wife to die in the hospital at Rouen. lie then went to live with a girl named Lefevre, and afterwards married her. They then commenced the magnetising trade. They established what they called a "Cabinet do consultations magnetiqucs" in the Rue de Seine, and made pompous advertisements of their skill in revealing secrets, curing diseases, giving information respecting persons and places, predicting the future, and all other feats of the magnetising fraternity. They, it appeared, made numerous dupes, their gains having amounted to f. 20,000 in the course of a year. They paid Grabowski, who described himself as a poor man without resources, f. 50 a month to sign the prescriptions. Their charge for each consultation was from f. 10 to CO. They also gave advice by correspondence, for which they were well paid. The most extravagant questions were put to them ; one was as to the means of making Paris a seaport ; and

several as to what was to be the future government of France; and the feconce paid, they answered each and all with becoming gravity. It further appeared that in some cases their pretended revelations caused profound discord in families. A 31. L emoine, a builder in the Faubourg St. Antoine, stated that his wife had consulted the ' sybille," and bad been told by her that he kept a mistress, and gave her f 300 a month and a house to live in. This drove his wife to despair, and it was for some time feared her mental faculties would be affected. To pacify her he at last went with her to the somnambulist, passing himself off as her brother. To his astonishment the "sybille" not only repeated her tale of his keeping a mistress, but actually gave liitu the name, address, and description of the person of the pretended mistress. The poor wife was in agony of mind, and, in the hope of convincing her that she was imposed on, lie took her to the address, and demanded the lady who had been named. It turned out that a lady of the name given actually lived in the house with her daughter. The poor builder told his story, and it naturally excited the lady's bitterest indignation. Her daughter, who was the person described by the somnambulist, almost fainted at hearing the abominable imputation cast on her. The lady and the daughter, however, accompanied the builder and his wife to the pretended sibyl, but in-

S 3f. C Ci'Jt X AT13. stead of being covered by confusion, as might have been expected, the woman asserted that they were mad, and that she knew nothing of them. The tribunal condemned the sibyl and her husband, who did not appear at the trial, to thirteen months' imprisonment; the Polish doctor to f5 fine. Sokolowski was discharged, as he only made up the medicines in the ordinary course of trade.

A Brahmin's Division of Proi>f.uty amongst his Widows. þÿ The East India papers by the last overland mail contain the following singular narrative : þÿ A curious case of the tyranny practised in native states, even when most strictly under the surveillance of the British government, has just come to light. þÿ Some years since a wealthy merchant at Baroda died, leaving two wives behind him ; the elder widow was of weakintellects, but had a son : the younger, a woman of talent and spirit, was four months advanced in pregnancy at the time of her bereavement. The husband willed that his property, amounting to above half a million sterling, should be life-rented in the widows, and that in the event of a boy being born it should be divided equally betwixt the children, the mothers being trustees over the whole till they were of age þÿ the survivor to inherit all in case of the decease of either. The Brahman died: five months afterwards his widow was delivered of a son. As the heritage was an enormous one, every precaution was taken to secure evidence of the genuineness of the child. Not the slightest doubts were raised on this subject for a year and a half, when the younger widow began to bring Baba, the manager of the estate, to account for extravagant conduct. While the child was out on an airing, it was stolen and carried into the wilderness, by Buba's directions, as is now allowed ; the mother was placed under personal restraint, and told she was an impostor þÿ that the child was

none of hers þÿ that hers had died in infancy. Remonstrance was in vain Ba- þÿ ba had now secured every channel of success to government by bribes or loans. At length a punchayet or jury of five was proposed : this at first, according to the advice of a native lawyer anxious to maintain litigation, the widow, strong in her consciousness of innocence, declined. A court of Baba's eleves was now constituted, and the case decided against her, þÿ no intimation having been to which she was to answer, the evidence supporting them, the record kept, or sentence pronounced. Repeated applications on the subject have hitherto only produced the answer that the case was closed þÿ Baba was content, so were his abettors : when did ever the cause of suffering awaken sympathy or arouse friends in the East, when the sufferer was poor and penniless ? The Bombay Government have at last been petitioned to take into consideration the new matter of the abduction of the child : Baba had no more right to make away with

an adopted child than with the offspring of the widow þÿ the theft offers the strongest presumption of his guilt. The senior widow is now said to repent of her ever having joined the prosecution against her sister, and to be anxious, if left to herself, to come into the field in her defence. fVell she may : if she dreams that her own offspring will ever see maturity, or she herself survive many years, she must look for a consummation unknown in oriental history. The family of the banker were under the protection of the British Government, and on this ground it is that we are specially bound to interfere þÿ either to secure for the widow her rights, or expose her as an impostor, if what has been stated should turn out incapable of proof ; and what is apprehended is the usual lazy answer by which injustice is soothed and ease secured þÿ "refer to previous decisions." The cruel Baba, at all events, deserves no mercy, unless child-stealing is to be formally sanctioned under authority of the British Government.

Curious Statement. þÿ It is stated that the building for the Exposition of 1851 will contain 500 miles of window sashes, 100 miles of putty, 24 miles of zinc guttering, 8 miles to drive under cover. The building will be wholly of glass, wood frame, and iron pillars. In one position the spectator will be able to see 1000 feet before him in one unbroken view. It is believed that the building will be so superb that the public on whose behalf the opposition has been made, will be the first to oppose its removal. A writer in the Bi ii.dek states that 150 tons of putty will be required to make the building."

An extraordinary change of fortune has just occurred to a young soldier of the 39th Regiment, at present stationed at Athlonc. By the death of an uncle in the island of Cuba, this young soldier has come into possession of 4)50,000, as is stated, in money, besides two valuable estates in the island. The young man's name is Marriott, and he is said to be a remarkably well-conducted person, of very agreeable manner, and only in the 20th year of his age, and had enlisted in the regiment as a drummer when only 13 years old. lie has left the regiment and is on his way to Cuba.

Extraordinary Transposition in Music. þÿ At one of the principal churches of Pesth, recently, the performance of the " Messiah" was appointed for a given her as to the charges charitable purpose. On the morning of the day appointed for the oratoria to be executed, it was discovered that the organ had been tuned exactly a semitone too high. This, as might naturally be supposed, would greatly distress some of the principal singers ; but how it was to be remedied no one could tell, until the organist, a Bohemian by birth, suggested that he should play the whole one-half note lower, and which he actually affected. Only thorough musicians can appreciate the difficulty of such a task, and the surprise was still greater at the facility of the performance.

In the þÿ St. Croix þÿAvis of 12th August last, which accompanies this sub No. I, is found inserted a so called þÿ Provisional þÿRescript for St. Croix, in regard to the right of selling Ac. Ac., dated General Government, St. Croix 30th July 1850, of which an English translation is published in a subsequent number of that paper. This Rescript, which announces its being operative on the 1st day of October next, lias awakened much trouble and anxiety among a great number of Your þÿMajesty subjects s on this island, namely, among that numerous indigent class in the towns, who in a great measure have earned a moderate and somewhat cumbersome subsistence by the exercise of that almost unlimited right ot trade hitherto existing and practised by the inhabitants, and which is designed to be abolished by this Rescript. Several hundred persons of the town of Christiansted have on this occasion selected us, the subscribers, to plead their cause, most submissively, to Your Majesty; the names of whom and the signatures of a part thus induced, accompany this sub No. 2. those peculiar relations ot St. briefly, We will presume to represent Croix, which according to our opinion have produced, to a certain extent, and still render necessary, a prolongation of this right of trade. The census of 13th May last shows that collectively Ihe population of St. Croix amounts to 23,720, whereof 8,250 appertain to the towns and 15,464 to the country. The proportion as 1 to some-
what less than 2.

8 ff AVI3 The proportion between women and men is for the towns þÿ Men 3,187 Women 5,009 a surplus therefore of 1,882 women or more than 58 per cent. This surplus is even greater in Christiansted 2,052 men to 3,318 women which gives a surplus of 1,200 women. In the country tbe surplus of women is not more than about 2 per cent. When we reflect that in the kingdom of Denmark the proportion between tbe population of the towns and country is about I to 5, it is assuredly very sui prising to see that here it is as 1 to 2. The proportion between men and women requires no comparison with any other place, as tbe general proportion, as tar as is known is a surplus of from 2 to 3 of women. If tbe grounds of these phenomena; are required, it is easily found in slavery, or more correctly speaking in the frequent exercise, during slavery, of tbe right appertaining to the slave of buying liis freedom, and which alter 1834 was restricted to a legal scale. The manumitted, whose number from among the rural population, was steadily on the increase, especially since 1834, moved into the Towns of Christiansted and Frederikstcd, as the Planters did not desire free laborers on tbe properties, nor were they themselves desirous of being subject to that uniformity oflabor, and that rigid discipline which partly the routine and perhaps also necessity had embodied in the culture thereof. It must here be noticed, that there is no land on the Island of St. Croix, that is not incorporated into some estate ;

and that the planters never have sold nor ever have been willing to sell land to the negroes or the manumitted. \\ liilst, therefore, the rural population decreased, the population of the towns thus proportionally increased. As means of livelihood in the towns were very limited, for naught but very inconsiderable handicrafts existed, and which even were restricted to the most common kind of tradesmen, such as Carpenters, Masons, Smiths, Shoemakers and Tailors, Ac. Ac., of which the productions of the three last, to an excess of half, are brought hither from foreign places ; and as no kind of commerce is carried on excepting what is caused by tbe export ot the þÿisland s industry, articles of necessity, it was a natural con- products, and the bringing hither of subsistence, aye! so important a part sequence that this repletion of tbe population of tbe towns, could not find means of livelihood. The better and more enterprising part namely, of the male population, abandoned tbe island, therefore, and went to St. Thomas or elsewhere, where means of subsistence more abundantly prevailed. That part of the town population which consisted of old people, invalids, women and children were constrained to remain behind ; women most especially, þÿ who in consequence of the deficiency of marriage ties þÿ a result of slavery þÿ had solely to provide for their offspring, and thus were hindered going to a strange place. The disproportion in the towns between men and women arose besides

from this, that a greater number of women than men of the rural population were bought free, and that the town slaves who went into the country were mostly men, who were eagerly bought by the planters during the last 10 years of slavery. That the disproportion between tbe population of town and country, and more so between men and women in the towns is an engenderment of slavery,

is shewn when we compare the different censa : they are as follows : þÿ Town population 1835 þÿ 8,321. 1841 þÿ 7,(w8. þÿ1840 7,452. þÿ1850 8,205. The town population of 1840 consisted þÿof 2,807 men, and 4,045 women, which gives the same proportion as the census of the present year, perluij s somewhat less. The same proportion existed after tbe census of 1835 and of 1841. When we, however, in Ihe census of 1840 take those above 15 years of age we find 1,008 men to 3,253 women, or above 100 per cent surplus. þÿ From the same census it was found, that the number of those in the towns, who lived by selling þÿ to be: Principals 390, and subordinates (probably children) 605. Handicraftsmen, 1710 principals, and 950 subordinates. þÿ The proportion here evinces but poorly tor the trader as each has about two persons to support; Handicraftsmen, on the c< i> trary, have scarcely the necessary proportion as only about every second' workman has but one person to maintain. þÿ Tbe numerals taken from these ccrsa may not be very accurate, the result, however, is probably very near the truth. This is, therefore, a natural inference, that the principal traders are chiefly women, and the handicraftsmen, men some w hereof arc young. As a sufficiency of feminine employments, such as housework, sewing, washing, and the like, could not lie, ami as a great many of these occupations which in other countries are performed I y women, were, in a state of slavery partly done by men, namely, house attendance,

cooking, and t lie like, it became imperative that a great many females should seek means of support for themselves and children in the making of bread, t lie selling it, also provisions, dressed and undressed, and manufactures þÿ in reality all articles usually sold en detail. I n't his traffic ail the indigent classes of the ticipate community þÿ widows and children of de- participated and still do pmceased officials, decayed plantt rs or their families, free persons of color, and the manumitted slaves þÿ especially the feminine part of these classes. Meanwhile the majority hereof, for a support, do not restrict iheinselves exclusively to any of these branches of as more than one of them forms a very important part of their that if deprived thereof ihe remainder would very inadequately furnish tbe common necessaries of life. '1 hese tiuders, consequently keep no store nor any settle d place of" sale, which premises something both of an assortment and well furnished stock ; and a fitting place of sale ; of w hich both essentials are naturally wanting, for the poverty of 1he individual prevents his getting the first, and the situation of bis dwelling þÿ in general at the outskirts of the tow i þÿ admits not any traffic. They therefore availed themselves of the only expedient þÿ that of carrying the articles from door to door, and tiius also extended this traffic into the country among the planters and laborers, and these itinerant sellers were mostly women. Very probably, to enable Ihe

Police, controlling to a certain extent, this traffic from being used as askrecn for criminal purposes, it was decreed that permission Ihus to carry about goods to sell should be obtained from the Police Magistrates who should issue such passes for a certain sum of money. This rescript was however far from being adhered to, but often used bj the Police to get a bold on such individuals, whom from other causes lliev fain would

strictly control. The number, therefore, of these passes, so issued, have ever been far below the number of those individuals, who either wholly or in part supported themselves as pedlars, or by employing others thus to sell for them. After the arrival here of the present Governor the carrying about of bread and cakes for sale was also made subjects of a permit, but here, also, the number of such who are registered, is very few compared to the number of individuals who follow this way oflivclihood. We have, in the course of a few hours inquiry, framed a list of such persons the the town of Christiansted who, in of short time premised we were enabled to ascertain, pursue this means of livelihood, and we presume to attach it sub No. 3, þÿ wherein is mentioned the names of those persons who at this present moment sell the bread they bake in sending it about, by means of 1)9 sellers þÿ this number however is far from being the real, which must not be regarded as but inconsiderably more. When the Government, therefore, in its þÿ Provisional þÿRescript,, points out that trade carried on in the way as premised, is accompanied by manifold inconveniences, and that it would be far more advantageous for the country if it were carried on differently, and that if a number of those persons so employed were otherwise engaged, say as agriculturalists, it is all very correct taken in the abstract, and it assuredly were very desirable that a better state of things could be instituted ; but it is also a

question if it is desirable nay feasible to cause a total alteration of all existing relations in the manner proposed or in any other sudden way? This can scarcely be called for when it is evident that a very large body of the population who have tlie prescriptive right of maintenance, in the way they are best acquainted with, and who are not fitted for and cannot obtain any employment more advantageous to the community at large, and who by this change are made liable to the greatest misery, aye! that of dying from hunger. It is a thing well known that, every v.dd a change in the means ot subsistence . mbodics manifold difficulties and distress for the laboring population, but when the condition of the working classes is very miserable and resources very few, it becomes almost a certainty that the greatest misery will ensue. Rut this Rescript even goes so far as not only to alter all commercial relations in the towns but also to take from them a great part of the trade which belongs to them. Tn the first whilst it decrees þÿ that trade must not he carried on in the country, but only in the þÿtowns, there is found simultaneously an exclusive right, far exceeding a common privilege, awarded the rural laborers, of trafficing with the principle articles of this trade þÿ such a privilege provisions is candles. Now granted to several when thousand persons, it must be asked what remains for the towns? and how this trade can so he controlled that all other things be not. made objects of traffic by

these persons? From report an endeavour of defence will lie made by Ibis, that pre-existing state they have only acknowledged of things, þÿ but this is a by no means the case. Fieldlaborcrs have never trafficed in provisions or the like articles; þÿ prior to emancipation provisions were delivered them by the planters who purchased them in the towns or partly ordered them from abroad in larger quantities ; in a great measure this has also been the ease since emancipation, and in any

®®<£>aa A T 2 3. contrary instance the laborer has in most cases purchased them in small quantities in the towns or from perambulating sellers or of individuals residing in the country which is particularly the case with bread. But even if the rural-population did carry on such a traffic it still appears strange to establish such a state of things in the country, whilst new taxes and restrictions are imposed on the towns and thus make an in itself pernicious custom, an established right by law. It is difficult to say whether this rescript will be most destructive to the towns or the country, although it is very evident that the lirst will immediately feel it, and the last only at a subsequent period. In respect to the country, it lies so near the towns that a desire to trade and huckster will withdraw the fieldlaborcrs attention from their chief occupation and make them had speculators instead of competent laborers. As regards the Town-people, there was a kind of hope prior to the issuing of this rescript, that some of them might be able to establish a retail trade in the country, for provisions and the like, when tlie laborers, which will very soon happen, receive their wages solely in Cash. When we presuppose a retail establishment for about every 200 persons and grants are principally restricted to such individuals of the towns-people who are recommended by the Magistracy, and who could make arrangements with some proprietor, as to a place of sale, it would create about 70 retailers

who, inclusive of children and assistants, would carry from 3 to 400 people into the country. The wish, nay, necessity, of such a vent for tlie towns is evinced by the numerals precedingly given. This hope, the rescript lias destroyed. Besides obstructing this expedient which appeared to open, tlie towns are now deprived the means of livelihood they formerly had in the retail trade. þÿ those who have gained a livelihood þÿ Tis true that the 7 decrees that, hitherto by carrying on trade in the towns, either from their own dwellings, or by itinerant sellers without being in possession of a þÿBurgher Brief, s shall also he entitled to carry on such trade in future in the towns and in their dwelling-houses, subject to a tax of from 81 to 5 þÿquarterly. It will, however, he seen from the preceding representation that this permission, to a great many, and those tlie most necessitous and helpless part of the population, will he perfectly illusory, as they neither possess means of procuring a stock of goods, or a good stand for a store, as little as the means of paying the tax, and, therefore, must stop pursuing their usual means of livelihood, and either become burthensome to the Poor-fund or perish from hunger. The prohibition of itinerant selling, especially bread and provisions, will, also, in another way, prove very oppressive to the indigent part of the population, as it prevents their getting in the easiest way, articles of necessity; this inconvenience is already severely felt in

the prohibition of an itinerant selling of fish. That the regulations in tlie þÿ Provisional þÿRescript, in as far as they do not carry along with them an enormous Pension-List of Paupers, will be advantageous, in the course of time, to the affluent class in tlie towns, is very possible ; but it assuredly must be considered a cruelty and an injustice against the Poor who are far more numerous : þÿ it

will complete what Emancipation and the New Tariff which imposes high duties on tlie chief necessities of lifeliave commenced. It can readily be conceived that tlie last has essentially been very oppressive to the poor classes especially in the towns, as their principal expense is in tlie purchase of those provisions, that formerly were duty free or subject to a very slight impost. Thus their usual food Iudian-Meal, formerly duty free, is now burthened with an impost of 10 per' Cent. II hen we assert that Emancipation has fallen most severely on the more indigent classes in the towns we must presume briefly to explain. A very considerable number of the town negroes were owned by the less affluent classes, white and colored ; the majority of whom had inherited them front their parents, who thus endeavored to procure their offspring a productive capital, which could not easily be raised in any other way, for tlie entire island was divided among 100 proprietors, who never, as precedingly remarked, were willing to alienate ever so small a part of their estates, hut have steadily endeavored to diminish the number of estates by tlieqoining of several in one. Without attempting to deny that the planters also may have lost by the Emancipation which has occurred, still tinloss even to the most disastrously situated has not been as great as to the town proprietor. The planter had his estate still left, to which his former slaves were attached, and he loses only in proportion to the higher þÿday wages, s which

lie may pay since emancipation. The town proprietor on the contrary has nothing left of his property, for by tlie emancipation of the slaves all his property has vanished. This especially concerns those who hired out the labor of their slaves for a certain sum monthly, hut which of course ceased with emancipation. To him who retained tlie services of his town or domestic slave, emancipation has not operated as disastrously, for wages, namely, for domestics have fallen, in at least 25 per cent or more, for when a well trained slave was hired as a domestic, monthly wages were from 87 to 88, whilst at present in a state of freedom from 85 to 0. The difference or something more went to the owner, in as far as lie hired out his slave, consequently, here also the indigent part of the population has suffered most. attach sub No. 4 þÿ We here presume, most humbly, to a draught drawn up by our legal adviser Lawyer II a i r \ r. n r. n n , and sent to the Burgher Council of this island in the month of January this year, concerning tlie effects of emancipation and the compensation-question, to which we express agreeing to in tlie main, and here repeat the wish therein expressed, that, the question as started may he investigated, as soon as possible, þÿ by competent and impartial men þÿ and that those arrangements relative to all branches of industry may be dormant, until such an investigation takes place. After having tints briefly expressed our most humble opinion as to tlie real nature of

flic þÿ Provisional þÿRescript issued hv the General Government, we take the liberty of uttering some doubts as to the authority of the Governor General, to issue it or any tiling like it. We are aware that the Ministry of Finance (vide Departements Tidendc of 27th October) in a communication of 2d July last, charges the Governor General not to avail himself of the authority given him by Vour Majesty in the instructions of 29th September 1848, to issue Provisional Rescripts, excepting on very important occasions, wherein the general

weal will not brook any delay, for example : civil commotions, hurricane &c. political and commercial embarrassments and the like, but in all other instances to send on proposals and draughts to the Ministry, that these might finally be decided on in the Mother Country. In this instance it appears that the Government have disregarded this order, and thus, it is presumed, gone beyond its authority. The rescript to be sure expresses its being issued subject to superior approval þÿ (which reservation, however, is left out in the English translation or expressed very vaguely) but as it must be supposed that it has first been sent home alter its date 30th July, it will be scarcely probabable that it can be looked into at home or that approval can be obtained so timely that Your þÿMajesty will s can be made known here prior to October. The Government therefore in this instance have acted on their responsibility, which on the whole appears to have been the intention, if one may judge from the brief notice and the manner of its notification. It becomes therefore a question whether such a pressing emergency is at hand as spoken of in the þÿMinistry com- s munication of 2nd July this vear? The M þÿinistry communication s openly refers to sudden occurring, unforeseen circumstances of a dangerous nature, but such are so far from being found, that on the contrary, the rescript in its preamble ol motives calls them evils which for a series of years have probably been pro-

duced from a state of things that existed from time immemorial. It has much disheartened Your Maþÿjesty s ubjects here resident, to see their most important interests so conspicuously, so perfectly, unauthorised, and according to their humble opinion in every instance, so destructively attacked by Your þÿMajesty s highest officials in the Colonies. Our firm confidence, only, in Your þÿMajesty just s and amiable character can sustain us under this trial as it permits us to hope that we shall obtain justice in this instance, and that those benefits will be awarded us which Ihe fundamental law has already afforded to Your þÿMajesty s subjects in the mother-country. In reference to which we will take the liberty here to remark, in as far the þÿ Provisional þÿRescript here spoken of might be recommended by the Burgher Council of St. Croix, that we cannot conceive those classes whom we now represent as represented in this Council, who are chosen by Proprietors in accordance to direct imposts, and who in reality solely consists of persons who cither belong to the class of planters or are of the monied interest. Only when a Burgher Council is elected by free suffrage or according to the same rules as those which are binding in an election to the Diet can we conceive the more indigent class of the population be secured against the pecuniary and landed interests here dominant. Whilst we onee more reiterate our conviction that it would be desirable that the relations of all branches of livelihood

be arranged in a way corresponding to the times, and that the present unlimited right of trade may be annulled in the course of time, but that it onght not to take place in the way which the Government have attempted, but in a manner that would not prove destructive to that portion of the existing population who tor a run of years have entirely or partly supported themselves by it, we will most humbly presume to petition that : I.) The þÿGovernment Provisional s Re script of 30th July last.be suspended

until further, and that no arrangements of this kind take place until a popular representation is effected. 2.) That Your Majesty will establish a standing representative council for the colonies in proportion to the Government, by the free election of the population, so that the indigent and much displaced part of the population may be represented. 3.) That the necessary steps be taken to carry the Fundamental Law into operation in the Colonies, Which has not even been promulgated here, and to institute an election to the Danish Diet. In case Your Majesty should consider it not feasible thus early to create a representation and that regulations of this nature he delayed, we then most humbly solicit þÿ That the General þÿGovernment sProvisional Rescript of 30th July last be suspended until further, and that the Provisional Rescript which might possibly be issued by Your Majesty may not conflict with the following: 1.) That all trade be restricted to the towns with the exception of such huckstering as may be considered ! ten 22de April 1817: necessary to furnish the rural population with pro visions, and that grants to form such retail shops be reserved for such individuals of the towns who may be considered most suitable. 2.) That the privilege of selling all kinds of goods by itinerant sellers, in the towns at least, he continued by all such persons who have hitherto either wholly or partly supported themselves in this way, and the requisite permission be given

by the Magistracy without payment and devoid of any impost on the trade. A delay of at least 1 2 mont hs þÿ after the date of such a law it is presumed should be awarded for paying lor a licence. 3.) That the baking of bread and the selling thereof either ir. dwellinghouses or by itinerant sellers to remain perfectly free both in town and country. Christiansted 23d September 1850. J. M. A general meeting of proprietors of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company was held in London on Thursday, when it dividend of £2 per share was declared for the last half year, free of income tax, payable on and after the 15th inst. The report of the directors was very satisfactory. The working account of the company exhibits an increase in receipts of £11,715, and a decrease of expenditure of £1707, making the surplus £13,481 Ids. 10,1. more than in the first half of the year 1841). The directors allude to the conclusion of the negocintions for the River Plate and Brazil packets, and the renewal of the contract for the service of the West India, Mexican, and South Americttn Mails, with her Majesty's Government. The Brazilian mail service will commence in the beginning of next year, for which five new ships are nearly ready for sea. The advantage in the saving of time by the present route to the West Indies, which commenced on the 2nd of August, is referred to, and the directors finally congratulate the proprietors upon the prospect of a full remuneration for their capital, enterprise, antl patience. The directors in their report go at some length into the proceedings hearing upon the contract, and state that all the books and papers of the company were submitted to Government to show

what profits had been made, and the issue was a contract for ten years, from the 1st January next, upon an annual payment for the tthole service of £270,000. The five new steam-ships for the Bra zil service will each be of 2250 tons and 800 horse power; and, when the new" ships perform the Atlantic voyages, the total acceleration will probably he twenty-two days out and home on the Jamaica route, thirty days on the Chagres, eighteen days on the Mexican, and eighteen days also on the British Guiana route. Fourteen steam vessels will he sufficient to perform the whole service after the 1st January next, and there will be three large ships besides in reserve. After severe trials in the infancy of ocean steam navigation, and the miscalculations and losses arising from the want of positive data, the company has at length obtained a prosperous state, and, with the prospect of a railroad across the isthmus of Panama and increased intercourse with the Pacific, there is no reason to doubt of its continuance. St. Thomas Times, Nov. 0, 1850. The Spanish Mail Steamship " G'alemma" of 459 horse power, lately purchased from the Canard Company by the Spanish Government, arrived in this port on the 2nd inst., having on hoard the newly appointed Captain-General of Cuba, his Excellency Senor Don Jose do la Concha þÿ Lieutenant-General in the Spanish service, «fcc. &c., his family, and staff, and the chief officers destined to serve under his command. His Excellency landed the same day at 4 o'clock p. m. when a salute of fifteen guns was fired from fort Christian, and a guard of honour under the command of Captain von Magens received him at the point of debarkation. His Ex. and family then repaired to the residence of Senor Don V. F- Segundo, H. M. Catholic Majesty's Consul at this port, whose hospitality they partook of during the remainder of their stay onshore. His Excellency embarked again on the 5th inst., when the same honors were paid him, as on the occasion of his reception in the island. The Caledonia, commanded by Lieut. Don Francisco Ramirez de Arellano, left Cadiz on the 16th Oct. and the Canary Islands on the 20th, and after a visit of three days steamed from this port on the 5th instant for Porto Rico and Havannn. This vessel also conveyed 450 soldiers with their respective officers, who compose a part of the force intended for the service of the island of Cuba, which will consist of 0000 troops ofboth infantry and artillery. His Excellency Senor Don Jose de la Concha has been appointed to the Gov-

ernment of Cuba in the place of the Conde dWlcov, who is at present in the administration of the Cuban Government. We understand it is in contemplation Tty the Spanish Government to establish a monthly mail communication between Cadiz and Havana, and that the Caledonia has been purchased with a view to this project.

Searles, the pedestrian, at Tramniere, completed bis arduous task of walking 1000 miles in 1000 hours on Monday morning, at seven o'clock, in the presence of a crowd of spectators anxious to see liim walk his thousandth mile. Just before starting a gentleman offered to wager JE 10 with the pedestrian that lie would not walk the mile under eight minutes. The wager was accepted by Searles, who started immediately after seven o'clock, and completed the mile in the extraordinary short space of 7 minutes and 41 srcm.N lie then ran

3 T. A7 18. once round the course with apparent ease, amid the cheering of the multitude. 4Ve believe that walking a mile in 7 minutes and 41 seconds stands unprecedented in pedestrian feats; and taking into account the difficult task which Searles had just completed, lie must certainly he reckoned as the swiftest pedestrian of the day, and his powers of endurance most extraordinary. In order to show that his physical strength was not exhausted, lie continued to walk a mile every hour up to four o'clock. þÿ He walked four miles backwards in the course of t he day, each of which lie completed under fifteen minutes. At four o'clock lie started backwards, and, notwithstanding the obstructions lie met Hot with from the crowd, he accomplished the mile in fourteen minutes and a quarter. lie then, at a quick pace, ran round the course, leaving his brother (who started with him) some distance behind. He was immediately raised upon the shoulders of some men and carried round the course, amidst the congratulations of the assembled crowd. At six o'clock an ample dinner was provided at Mrs. Fernyliough's hotel, at which a number fortnight of the pedestrian's friends sat down, and did justice to the fare provided It was intended to finish the affair by a grand display of fireworks, hut this was prevented by a heavy and continuous fall of rain.

An " Infernal Machine." þÿ On Friday a wooden box was received through the post by Mr. Frederick F.ast, son of a leather manufacturer, Bermondsey- in street, Southwark. As some gunpowder fell out on the lid being partially raised, suspicion was excited, and it was not opened until it had been well drenched with water. It contained nearly a pound of the finest gunpowder, with irregular pieces of lead, and just underneath the lid were a number of lucifer matches and sandpaper placed in such a position that the least violence used in forcing up the top of the box must lead to an explosion of the whole contents of the interior. No clue has yet been obtained to the wretch by whom it was forwarded.

A chasseur. named Fabre, was tried 011 Friday before the second council of war, for having insulted a guard of the gendarmerie mobile, and, in addition, for having wounded with his sabre the same and a serjeant-major. The evidence was very simple, and altogether conclusive against the prisoner. The guard was passing along the Avenue Lowendal, when the prisoner and another sol dier approached, and the former applied to him an insulting epithet. The prisoner, on being remonstrated with, struck the guard with his sword on the head and drew blood, the stroke being fortunately deadened by the shake of the wearer The two soldiers then took to flight, and a serjeant-niajor seeing a man in uniform running along with a drawn Weapon in his hand, attempted to bar his passage. The prisoner at once stiuck at him with the sword, and wounded him in the side of the head. þÿ It was proved, also, that the prisoner wns known in the regiment as an illtempered, quarrelsome fellow. THE PEDIGREE OF WASHINGTON. A few copies of a beautiful illuminated sheet, drawn by Mapleson, the editor of " Pearls of American Poetry" and ' The Shakspeare Ballads,' have just been received. The Pedigree of General Washington, ns traced and illuminated by Mr. Mapleson, carries hack his descent to William de ller'hu n, Lord of the Manor of W ashington, in the county of Durham. England. From him descended John Washington, of Whitfield, in the time of Richard III; and ninth in descent from the said John, was George, first President of the United States. The mother of the John Washington who emigrated to Virginia in 1657, and who was greatgrandfather to the General, was Elanor Hastings, daughter and heiress of John Hastings, grandson to Francis, second Earl of Huntingdon. She was the descendant, through Lady Huntingdon, of George, Duke of Clarence, brother to King Edward IV., and King Richard III. by Isabel Newill, daughter and heiress of Richard, Earl of Warwick, the Kingmaker. Washington, therefore, as well as all the descendants of that marriage, are entitled to quarter the arms of Hustings, þÿ Pule, Earl of Salisbury, Plantagenet, Scotland, Flortimer, Earl of March, Newill, Montagu, Beauchamp, and Devereux. þÿ Boston Transcript.

Hamburg, Oct. 7. þÿ Before this can arrive, intelligence will have reached London that the bombast and bombarding of the insurrectionary forces lias terminated in their complete discomfiture, and that, after seven days of most unremitting efforts and a most undoubted display of courage, they have been compelled to " break off" the combat and retire whence they came, not only with most serious loss, hut with no oilier advantage to themselves or the cause of the rebellion, than the capture of those worthless falconets, and their having, it may lie said, wilfully and wantonly bombarded, ruined, and burned down sundry portions of a flourishing

ST <8 t> 3 AT2 town, inhabited by their own countrymen, some of whose lives are said to have been sacrificed, whilst the property of a much greater number has been damaged or completely destroyed. Certainty of success, and certainty of being enabled to recompense the sufferers for their losses, could scarcely have justified the insurrectionary chiefs in proceeding to this calamitous extremity, which, it is needless to add, is only resorted to in war when assailing generals have to deal with hostile populations, or under circumstances of extremest urgency. It has been repeatedly stated, in previous communications, that one of the most serious obstacles to the attainment of accord between the Danes and Holsteiners was the command of the liolstein army brigades and departments being in the hands of officers who are strangers to and have no other interest in the land or its cause, than the pretext of German rights, no other ties than connection of Germanic races ; and who, being moved by the impetus natural to impatient and ambitious soldiers, have plainly proved at Fredcrickstadt tiiat tiiese impulses were superior to all considerations for the interests, all regard lor the lives and property of the inhabitants þÿ although we have been told, with rare coolness, that the inhabitants begged General Willisen not to spare their town. Stress is laid upon tins subject because there was not a llolstein, Hamburg or German journal, which did not break forth in bitter vituperation at the "brutal ferocity" of the

movement with trifling loss compared to that of their enemies, and have resumed their old positions, ready to advance again full of ardour to receive a fourth proof that the Danish troops are as valiant and steadfast in defence, as they showed themselves ardent and resolute in the attack at Idstedt. It appeared evident, from the first day the operations commenced, that the Danish General felt confident that the garrison of Frederickstadt could maintain its ground, although holding an open town, or that, when the propitious moment arrived, he would move down to their assistance, and endeavour to catch the assailants between two fires, if they threw themselves into a position to be attacked in the rear. In the absence of details all that can be looked are results, and which are the more honourable to the Danish detachment, when it is considered that Frederickstadt is what may be termed an open place þÿ that its only defences are earthworks and temporary rf.dipps, or blockhouses, thrown up hastily within the last six weeks þÿ that it lias no regular ramparts or scarps þÿ that between forty and til'ty guns, some of the heaviest calibre, were brought to hear upon it þÿ that the garrison w ere harassed I v the necessity of extinguishing fires, a s well as by that of working night and day in strengthening their week defences, which mainly depended on the contiguous wet ditches and marshy ground on the land side, and upon the high dykes ofi the right Eider hank, which latter served as a shelter against point-blank though not again- 1 ricochet firing. It must also he added, that the artillery at the disposal ofi tiie Dani>ii commandant was deficient in number and calibre, comparatively speaking, with that ofibiassailants ; that he was obliged to husband bis ammunition, and that from the low situation ofi the town he could not return his enemy's fire, poured from the gun-boats and the opposite Eider hank, with any good effect. to success þÿ for holding out and eventually repulsing an enemy, who commenced his operations, and valiantly and actively carried them on, under a conviction that the Danish garrison would lie an easy prize, or Miat it would fly and abandon the place. The bombast and trash published by the Hamburg and llolstein journals, and thence iiltered through the German press, have exceeded everything we have had before of this nature, since the dav when the defeat and (light from ldstcdt was declared to have been a mere " breaking oil" ol battle, tor the purpose of taking up a better position. We must now be prepared to hear that the causes for " breaking off" the attack on Fredcrickstadt were the unfavourable state of the weather, which has certainly been most unpropitious þÿ the discovery that I the place was stronger than was anticipated þÿ the impossibility of undertaking regular siege operations by parallel trench, approaches, and sap, and of arming breaching batteries on marshy ground; that the Danes had men and guns double in number to those at the disposal of llolstein ; that the retreat has been a mere withdrawal þÿ a nun i.er Polk miki'x s.u tr.n þÿ and not a consummate repulse; and, fourthly, that the injury done by the bombardment is comparatively trilling, and the loss of the Danes immense. prise which it commenced under every declaration of overweening confidence and s irecss. Partly from the tactical < errors on the part of Willisen, and part- j h by sheer force and endurance on that I equally þÿ indeed, they of the Danes, the llolsteiners were discomfited and driven back upon the 25th of July. I pon the I'itli of September they endeavoured to retrieve these erand ill-advised attack on the Danish | by rors and their conscquetfc.es by a bold right Hank, and were again defeated. þÿ I pon the 29th of September, nnd during seven subsequent days, they made a third ellurt, which, no matter what the cause, has been equally unsuccessful. þÿ Tims, having been beaten in tlioir ad- I vanced (rout in Julv, beaten on their ! right in September, beaten on their left in October, nothing remains for ihe insurrectionary forces to complete the cube of dangerous essays than to attempt a desperate rush upon the Danish main position, or to wait patiently, as would have been more prudent, until winter hardens the surface of the land, and deprives the Danes of their allies þÿ the waters. As before said, we have no details of the immediate operations or causes which led to the forced abandonment ol the attack, which abandonment, it is superfluous to observe, would not have occurred had there been a chance of success, or had not the assailants been repulsed with heavy loss. Till: STATE OF EUROPE. Loxnox, Oct. 25, 1859. The intelligence I have to transmit to you by the present mail, is of a most important character. At no time since the last French revolution, has the state of Europe been so critical as at the present moment. It is still to be hoped that t lie peace of Europe will not be disturbed; but the deadly weapon of war is loaded, and it is on a hair trigger, which the slightest touch will set off. France must cede the step to-daj in point of importance to the affairs of Germany. The duration of the war between Denmark and the Duchies, fa von d by Germany, in face of a treaty of peace signed with Prussia, with no prospect of a cession of bloodshed, has at length induced two of the great powers to take a most important and serious step with

regard to Prussia. Other political motives have doubtless urged them to do so. France and Russia have threatened to enter Germany, sword in hand, if the pence with Denmark is not speedily acted upon according to the treaty, and the London protocol. On Wednesday afternoon last, a cabinet council was held at the foreign office. The following ministers were present : þÿ Lord John Russell, Lord Palinerston, the Lord Chancellor, Marquis of Lansdowne, Sir George Grey, Earl Grey, Sir Francis Baring, (First Lord of the Admiralty,) Mr.Lahouchere, Sir John 1 lohhouse, and the Marquis of Clanricarde. \\ hat took place at the council was communicated to the Times, which journal next morning published the following : þÿ The cabinet, which would not otherwise have assembled till the Gth of next month, met yesterday, at a very short notice, on a question of considerable urgency. The disgraceful conduct of Prussia, in helping to protect the Schleswigllolstein war, not only in spite of a treaty of peace with Denmark, but actually under cover of the treaty, and by means of it has led to a very natural þÿ we might almost say legitimate þÿ consequence. þÿ The Governments of Russia and of France have jointly proposed to the government of this country, that the three powers shall peremptorily require Prussia to fulfil her recent engagement with Denmark, and withdraw the support she still continues to give to the Schleswig-Ilolstein army. In the event of Prussia hesitating to comply with

this reasonable demand, Russia and France arc proposed to back it, not by an unprofitable march to the territory under dispute, but in a way more congenial to their tastes þÿ by an invasion of the Silesian provinces of Prussia on the one side and the Rhenish on the other. In the first instance, however, they require the co-operation of England in the remonstrance with Prussia, without which they arc not prepared to move at present. The answer of the British government may perhaps be anticipated. It declines to join with Russia As France in such a note as we have described, but proposes that all three powers shall separately remonstrate with Prussia on her present breach of faith with the Danish government. Whether their triple remonstrances will be of more avail than all the rest of the diplomacy that has been lavished on this affair, is a question on which we will not venture to give an opinion. The funds immediately declined d-8ths, and there will be a similar depression elsewhere.

At the date of my last letter 1 advised of the advance of the Holstein troops, the object of which does not appear even yet to have been clearly ascertained, but the result has been such as to shew that the Danish trenches were not to be so easily carried, and the Holsteiners have been gl.id to return to their old quarters. The movements since of neither party have been of any importance, excepting that the Danes have taken possession of the islatidson the west coastofSchleswig after a sharp action which took place on the 17th inst., between some Holstein gun-boats and two Danish steam ships. Tae lloistetn party seem by their repot is to have been surprised at the ' great skill'' with which the Danish works were constructed, and Major Wynekt.t late soi s-chek of General Williscn has entirely quitted the Holstein si rviee, having been opposed to the attack on the Danish lines, the result of which lias justified him. A great desire is now manifested even in Copenhagen for a conclusion to this absurd war; the "Post" there regrets l that idstedt was not the last conflict and urges the Danish government to take measures to render the London protocol and l lie Rerun treaty realities þÿ perhaps in after all however this entreating system mid the quiet course of events may as in Lord Wellington's case at Santarem bring about this desirable event sooner than we at present expect ;þÿ a deputation from the Peace Society have taken it upon them to visit the belligerents

and a graphic account is given in the Times of their proceedings as bearing on the general peace question, but they have evidently although unconsciously taken a side, and while common politeness causes such a mission to be courteously received by both parties, it does not promise much. ##

AFRICA. The Bouelta brigantme arrived at Portsmouth on Saturday from the coast of Africa, where she has been nearly three years in commission. Her commander, Lieutenant Forbes, has been employed during the past year in negotiating with the King of Dahomey, in the endeavour to establish a treaty for the abolition of the slave trade throughout his territory, hut which failed. His Majesty reviewed his troops during Commander Forbes' sojourn with him, and they are spoken of as well disciplincd, though 4000 out of 10,000 of the soldiery are women clothed as men, who perform their military duties in every respect as well as their male companions arms. His Majesty as a mark of his especial favour, presented Commander Forbes with a juvenile princess, aged seven years, whom he has brought to England to be educated. At the "Customs" (a sort of religious rite) 30 human sacrifices were offered lo their deity, two of these (soldiers from Attapalimc, aged respectively 40 and 50) Commander Forbes purchased for 8 100, and sent to Fernando Po to he liberated. The slave trade was very brisk, and the squadron very healthy. An inspection ol the Government steamers at Woolwich is in progress, it being intended to have 32 steam-vessels constantly employed for the suppression of the slave trade on the coast of Africa; one of these vessels being ordered to proceed about the 1st of every month with the mails, and relieve another from duty on the coast. The sailing vessels at present on the African station arc to

he withdrawn as soon as steamers are ready to replace them, and no sailing vessels will in future he employed fox the suppression of the slave trade. A shock of an earthquake was felt at Algiers on the night of the 10th inst. þÿ It lasted 15 seconds. This makes t he sixth shock which has occurred within 10 days. þÿ Wilmcr &. Smith's Times.

MARSHAL HAYNAU. It will not, perhaps, be altogether out of place to remind the reader of a fewstriking particulars of the career of blood pursued by this monster in Hungary. Take for example the execution of thirteen Hungarian officers, of the first rank and highest character, in cold blood, on the 6th of October, 1819, after the for ever-accursed Ireachcry of Gor gov had compelled bos bravp tnn 4r

surrender to the Austrians. It is from the pen of an eye-witness. Ex uno DiscE omnes: þÿ " Four of these heroic men met their end by day-break, the commutation of their sentence to ' powder and lead' exempting them from the anguish of witnessing the death of their companions in arms. Amongst the rest was Ernest Kiss. His brother had become insane after Gorgey's treachery ; bis cousin had fallen, a second Leonidas, in defence of the Rothenthnrm Pass; be himself, the richest landed proprietor in the Banat, whose hospitable castle was all the year round filled with Austrian cavaliers and officers, was on the 6th of October sentenced to death by the Austrian court-martial, on which sat many of the former partakers of his hospitality. His friends at Vienna had Temeswar. interceded to save his life, but in vain. þÿ He died a painful death ; the Austrian soldiers who were ordered to carry the sentence into effect, and who for a whole year had faced the fire of the Hungarian artillery, trembled before their defence- hut ess victim ; three separate vollies were tired before Iviss fell þÿ his death-struggles lasted full ten minutes. The report of the firing was heard, in the castle, where those officers sentenced to be hung were preparing for death. Poltenberg had been in a profound sleep ; and startled, as he told the Austrian officer, by the first volley, he had jumped out of bed. The unhappy man had been dreaming that lie was in the face of the enemy, and heard the firing of

alarm signals at his outposts þÿ it was he summons from the grave. At six o'clock in the morning the condemned officers were led to the place of execution. Old Aulich died first; he was the most advanced in years, and the courtinartial seemed thus to respect the nairal privilege of age. Distinguished by his zeal and efforts in the cause of nau, and the outbreak of some petty dishis country, more than by the success which attended him. Aulich was inferior to many of his comrades in point of talent ; but in uprightness and strength of character none surpassed him. Count Leiningen was the third in succession ;.nd the youngest. An opportunity had been offered hiin on the preceding evening of escaping by flight ; but he would not. separate his fate from that of his brother-in-law, who was a prisoner in the fortress. His youth, perhaps, inspired him with a desire of giving to his elder companions in sorrow around him an example of heroic stoicism in death ; and. on reaching the place of xecution, exclaimed with mclaucho- he ly honour, They ought at least to have ' treated us to a breakfast !' One of the guard of soldiers compassionately handed him his wine flask. ' Thank you, my friend,' said the young general. ' I want no wine to give me courage þÿ bring me a glass of water.' He then wrote on his knee with a pencil the following fare-well words to his brother-in-law: þÿ ' The shots which Ibis morning laid my poor comrades low still resound in my cars, and before nic hangs the body of
Vulich on flic gallows. In this solemn

I « C 31 D 1 3 A T 2 $S« moment, when 1 must prepare to appear before my Creator, I once more protest against the charges of cruelty at the taking of Buda, which an infamous slanderer has raised against me. I commend to you my poor Liska and my two children. I die for a cause which always appeared to me just and holy. If in happier days my friends ever desire to avenge my death, let them recollect that As for' - - - humanity is the best political wisdom. þÿ - here the hangman interrupted him. It was time to die. Torok Laliner, Polenberg, Nagy Sandor, Knezich, died one after the other. Veesey was the last ; perhaps they wished, by this nine-fold aggravation of his torments, to ni.ike him suffer for the destruction caused by his cannon at Damianich preceded him. The usual dark colour of his large features was heightened by rage and impatience. His view had never extended further than the glittering point of his heavy sabre ; this was the star which he had followed throughout life ; now he saw whither it had conducted him, and impatiently exclaimed, when limping, up to the gallows, ' Why is it that I, who have always been foremost to face the enemy's fire, must here be last?' The deliberate slowness of the work of butchery seemed to disconcert him more than the approach of death, which he had defied in a hundred battles. This terrible scene lasted from six until nine o'clock." A solemn funeral service for the repose of the soul of Louis Philippe was celebrated on the 11th ultimo, in the Church of St. Joseph, at Marseilles. A great crowd attended. The members of the sanitary commission recently named by the Government had a place in the choir. The Herald's correspondent learns that negotiations are about to be opened between Spain on the one side, and England, France, and Holland on the other, hy which the former on condition of having Cuba protected hy the joint action of that state, engages to pay the debt due hy Spain to English, French, and Dutch claimants. The reported changes in the Ministry are unfounded. The new ship of the line La Ville de Paris, 120 guns, will be launched on the 5th of this month. The keel of this ship was laid in 107 ; and another ship of the line, still on the stocks, the Louis XIV., was laid in 1801.

SPAIN. Private letters from Madrid, of the 18th ult., state that the Captain-General of Puerto Rico had demanded the creation of a permanent commission, like that at Cuba, for the framing a new Customs' tariff and had himself proposed several important modifications relative to the import duties. It was believed at Madrid that Shelley, the present Captain-General of Andulasia, would he the new Inspector-General of Cavalry, the same objections continuing against General Serrano. Orders have been sent to Cadiz to prepare the Columbus to take 000 soldiers to Cuba in all haste. It was reported in the best informed cireles in Madrid that the Queen had presented the decoration of the Golden Fleece to the President of the French Republic. The appointment of General Don Jose de la Concha to the command of t lie island of Cuba has been confirmed by a special decree. The departure of the troops composing the expedition is fixed for the 15th of October. The two steam vessels now in England, with others belonging to the Royal Navy, and some merchant vessels, are to proceed immediately to Cadiz to receive the troops and the military stores which are in that part. Letters from Cadiz announce the arrival there of the magnificent steamer the Caledonia, purchased in England by the Spanish Government. Site performed the passage from Liverpool to Cadiz in 125 hours. The troops intended for the island of Cuba are marching from all directions to the points destined for their embark-

ation. They are perfectly equipped, and in a superior condition as regards instruction and discipline. The points of departure arc Cadiz, Barcelona, and Santander, and the expedition sails about the middle of October. þÿ lb

Building in the air. þÿ A Frenchman has proposed an aerial scheme for a suspension bridge from Calais to Dover. þÿ The platform lie proposes to support at each end hy piers, the intermediate way to lie carried past and supported on chains held up in t lie air by balloons, and moored to sunken buoys. Over this air supported platform lie would drive an atmospheric railway. How his balloons are to be kept steady he does not say. Neither are we informed how the storms are to he prevented from tearing them to tatters. The Academy of Sciences, however, we are informed, are considering the plan.

The captain, it is said, immediately ordered the boats (of which there were only two) to be lowered, when with some half dozen be got into one of them. A Bonaparte in Troubi þÿr.. A despatch from Marseilles, dated Sunday, states that Pierre Bonaparte, representative of the people, and brother ot the

Prince of Caniuo, embarked at that place on the 20th for Corsica. Pierre Bonaparte would appear fated to be always getting into scrapes. During his journey from Avignon to Marseilles he got into a dispute with one of his fellow-travellers whom he met at the ailroad station at Tarascon. The discussion, which, however, is said to have been of a personal, and not of a political, nature, became very angry, so much so that blows were exchanged, and it was feared that Pierre Bonaparte would make use of the weapon he had with hun, namely, a double-barrel gun, a sixbarrel pistol, and a poniard. In the way of arms this was rather a handsome supjily for one man. The parties were separated, and arrangements were made for a duel the next morning. The matter, however, was finally arranged by mutual friends "to the honour of both," as the dispatch mentions, and Pierre continued his journey to Corsica, embarking on the 20th for Marseilles. The other party had not been aware at first that his antagonist was a member of the Bonaparte family and a cousin of the President of the Republic.

Accustomed as our transatlantic cousins are to expect everything and to claim everything, they little thought five years ago that tliey would so soon occupy the western coast, be the lords of the Pacific, ami possess a city there whose sudden rise surpasses even the imperial creations of Constantinople and Alexandria. They are quite beside themselves with wonderment and joy. So confident are they that everything is working in their favour þÿ so firm are they in the persuasion of their destiny »o fill the New World and hold the balance of the Old, that they are beginning to be indifferent, or rather carelessly unanimous as to ordinary questions. The cry is, " Let's have a struments, furniture, settlement any how, that we may push altogether for the great game before us." flie questions of slavery, of the Texan and New Mexican boundaries, of the Californian constitution, and even of the tariff, have all been hurried or slurred over. One thing they say they must have, and that without delay þÿ a railway or a canal through the Isthmus. By this and by an electric telegraph through Mexico they expect soon to bring San Francisco as near to New York as New Orleans was a few years ago. Preparations are already in progress for shipbuilding in Oregon in order to save the passage round Cape Horn. Even the overland route is beginning to lose its terrors. The Mormons are forming settlements just at the point where they will prove most serviceable to the exhausted caravans; and before very long

it is by no means impossible that a railway may connect New \ ork and San Francisco. In the midst of these brilliant prospects it is very natural that the citizens of the Union should show even less than their usual þÿmodesty.

Q m 0 2 Z AT 2 But the same prudence which should lead them to moderate their hopes suggests to us also not to do this for them. It is not for us to say what destiny is or is not in store for thein. When the present is so far out of human calculation, which is more likely than that the future should be also ? þÿ London Times

French Gluttony. þÿ A very erroneous notion generally prevails that the French are in general persons of very meagre appetite. The proceedings of "a party of four," as recorded in the Paris papers, will disabuse our readers of this fallacious idea: þÿ A farmer near Meaux had, it appears, sold in the morning some straw for 200 f. : in the Rue Ruinbeuuteau lu met three comrades of his, whom lie had known formerly in Algeria. The farmer offered to give them a breakfast, and they all proceeded to the Rue Montorgneil for the purpose. They intended to eat a few dozen of oysters and acotelette, hut l'appetit vient en mangeant; and, after 22 dozens of oysters had disappeared, each man took a potage and two cotelettes ; they then disposed of a salmi of four partridges, next two crayfish, eight roast partridges, a dessert to match, and 23 bottles of wine. The hill amounted to 11)7., the waiter received 3!'., and so the 2 )01'., had disappeared.

St. Thomas Times, Oct. 30, 1850. In our journals of the 26th ami present date will he found a notice from our Chief of Police, respecting measures to be adopted to promote the health and cleanliness of the town. The cholera being now in the West Indies, it behoves all persons, as far as lies m their power, to aid 1 lie very prudent measures by the civil authoriin order to prevent, by every timely precaution that human foresight can be placed can adopt, so dreadful, so fatal a disease from gaining a footing among us. Prevention is better than cure, therefore a strict attention to the spirit of the notice we publish, will go far to protect the community from so fatal a Tuesday the 19th for the inhabitants visitant, and will most certainly tend to mitigate its effects and abbreviate its stay, in the event ol its appearance in tlie island. Should cholera break out among us, wc must expect to see our harbour in a great measure deserted, and the activity of commerce lessened ; this though unquestionably a great evil, is comparatively nothing, when we consider the more lasting afflictions it is calculated to entail on us, the heart-rending þÿbereavements the sweet lies of affection rudely sundered the heart deeply lascerated by the loss of those whom we were accustom- Wednesday the 27th for ditto in West- istence, or the soother of our earthly successful, and which renders the cure ed lo look up to, as the stay of our excares þÿ the parent mourning for the sweet blossoms that shed their fragrance round his dwelling þÿ the wife for the

Wednesday the 27th for the inhabi- playmate of her earliest days ; in short ter Through husband of her youth þÿ the sister for the every tie that binds man to his kind, severed, and its finest links broken. þÿ a These are the great evils that we are called on to guard against, and may the appeal not be made to us in vain ; may we be spared by a strict and timely attention to the few and simple measures of precaution urged on us, from a calamity so dreadful in its effects. It is true that cholera has not yet made its appearance among us, that not a single case of illness similar in its symptoms, lias occurred in the island, but we cannot say how long we shall be free from it þÿ its progress is always rapid and unaccountable, and it is thought to have its origin in the impurity of the atmosphere. The West Indies have hitherto fore been spared its ravages ; but now that it lias arrived at Jamaica, we should not shut our eyes to the probability which exists, that unless every prudent means he taken, we may bitterly have to regret the neglect of a few necessary and timely precautions þÿ precautions, in themselves, necessary at all times, imperatively so at the present crisis. All decayed vegetable matter, offal, and putrescent substances, should be removed from the town, and should on no account whatever he allowed to accumulate in the vicinity ; quick lime will be found highly beneficial in places where such removal is impossible : this, with strict attention to the cleanliness of per-
son þÿ temperate and wholesome diet þÿ and a free and moderately open state of

the system þÿ are perhaps amongst the most important and efficacious means of prevention. Those who have already witnessed the effects of this disease, the fearful loss of life it occasions, the dread, tbe tear that possesses all where it is known; those persons, will require no inducement to further by every means in their power, any measures that may þÿ tend to prevent its dreaded K midst of life we are in þÿdeath appearance. saith the scriptures þÿ and certainly man " bich that great truth is more in no position in life, in startingly brought home to hint than in a large I city where this scourge is pursuing its | dreadful ravages. The þÿ uncertainty of þÿlife is there a manifest reality, its lessons forced continually his mind ; his on leelings, awakened by the very selfishness of his nature, show him the frailty of that present life he so highly prizes, which a tew hours illness can so quickly mar ; and turns him from the contemplation of the busy future of this world, greatly to entertain a thought of the dread eternity of the next.
