D. detailing a mode of treatment, which is said to have proved eminently
of cholera, under medical supervision, as certain as that of ordinary diseases. We shall publish the extract in our next.

EUROPEAN TIMES. Liverpool, October 17. DENMARK and THE DUCHIES. The Holsteiners, on the morning of the 20th, made an attack on Frederichstadt. At Suderatapel and both banks of the Eyder an irregular cannonade continued throughout the day. At five in the afternoon part of the town bad been set on fire, but up till ten at night bad not been taken. Tonning was occupied by the Holsteiners, who had made 217 prisoners.

The Kolner Zeitung, of Wednesday- , has a telegraphic despatch from Ham- j spoken of was nearer 5u0 than 300 lmrgh of the 30tli ult., stating that the Schleswig- llolsteiners had attacked and carried with the bayonet two of the entrenchments of Frederichstadt. They took 14 pieces of artillery. The Schleswig-Holstein army attempted to take Fricdrichstadt hy storm, at 4 p. m. on the 5th, but were repulsed by the Danes. The army of the Duchies is in position at Sunderstapel. Its loss is considerable, particularly in officers. Our dates from the seat of war are to the morning of the 5th inst. After bombarding part of the town during the preceding day, and after destroying the large block house close to the road, the town was in the evening attacked by two battalions of infantry and a detachment of riflemen. The principal church was burning at the time, and one end of the town was one complete mass of flame. After a desperate struggle, in which both sides must have experienced very heavy losses, the Danes gave way a little but only to seek the cover of new entrenchments and barricades thrown up in the middle of the town The resistance which they met with here was so violent and determined, that, notwithstanding the most brilliant bravery, the Schleswig- llolsteiners were compelled to retire from the town at midnight. They took up newposition a somewhat in advance of the old, and the conflict was to be renewed on the following morning. The losses sustained by the Schleswig-

Holsteiners arc as yet unknown. Both sides behaved extremely well, according to the accounts. General Willisen issued the following report on the first assault of Frcidrichstadt ; it is dated Sunderstapel, October 4, nine p. m. : þÿ þÿ Having completed the necessary preparations for storming Fricdrichstadt, the llolsteiners would withdraw the attack took place this evening, and has been conducted with so much bravery by the troops that, under less disadvantageous circumstances, success must have been inevitable. The troops, however, fell in large numbers, partly in the trendies, which it was necessary to bridge over just under the þÿenemy s fire, and partly amongst the half-ruined works, behind which the enemy sheltered himself, and kept up a discharge of shot upon our columns ; so that, in spite of the brilliant valour of our men, it was impossible to obtain possession of the place. The enemy persist in the defence with constancy. It has been impossible to avoid burning a large portion of the city. These events will not exercise any decisive influence upon the progress of the war. \V e have the following correspon- j dence relating to the second attack dated Hamburg, October (I : þÿ þÿ The Schleswig-Holstein corps lias again made an attempt to storm Frederichstadt, and with no better success. The troops retired last night to a position between Sunderstapel, and Set lie, with a loss of six hundred men. The withdrawal was covered by the Christiansen battery, and lighted by the flames of the burning city. 1 talked to-day with a soldier who was j one in the assailing corps. He spoke of the block-houses and entrenchments which the Danes had constructed at Friederichstadt, as bulwarks so impregnable that the cannon-shot had no effect upon them. After storming one bleach, the troops would push on, believing that the way was clear, when suddenly a whole succession of new works became visible. The drum was incessantly beaten to the attack ; assaults followed assaults, but all in vain. The bullets flew round like bail, while the burning houses sent out a scorching heat. A bridge broke with a number of men on it; nearly all perished. Carelessness was imputable, for no officer should have trusted approaches left by þÿ the enemy. The garrison of Friederichstadt, originally consisting of three bntallions had been considerably inereas- j ed. The communications with llusum have been almost uninterruptedly main- ! tained, and Danes have been seen marching to and fro these three days. The colonel of the Cth battalion has been taken prisoner by the þÿDanes.

Our letters of the 7th instant contain only the confirmation of the report of J the storming of Friederichstadt, and further details. It was expected that from before the place, as they could not invest it from the north and west. Half the town is destroyed. The Holstein army is to be increased by four battalions, or more than 5000 men. The failure of the attempt to carry the fortifications of Frederichstadt by j storm lias been followed by a withdrawal of the troops to their encampment, and the removal of the heavy guns to Rendsburg. The farthest point to which the llolsteiners penetrated during the assault was to the Uorkhuhle, where they were stopped by the pallisades. They did not enter the market j place, as stated. It will probably appear that General Willisen has not increased his military reputation by this affair.

It never entered into any reasonable þÿman b s ead þÿ1ba ditto in i file Danish general would look on with indifference, ami permit three or four battalions to lie eut up or cut off without moving to their þÿsupport that is, if they inquired assistance. All we know up to the present moment of the affair is the repul,,- of the assailants. This is not only t., tit, no matter how limited or greal tlo- loss io the latter or to the Danes, hut most important in a military and moral point of view ; for it proves that the 11-dstein commanders, to say tin: least of them, are consummately unsuccessful and unlucky þÿ fatal qualities in þÿcommanders and that, how ever brave, ardent, and reckless tin heterogeneous Holstein army max bt ,

it finds an insuperable harrier in the ters than the Ilolsteinors have hitherto encountered to þÿ heat the eoneeit out of them ; þÿ hut it nevertheless cannot f, to create in the minds of their eon m inders more respect for their adver ries, and show them that tampering with Persons neglecting to produce the iufnin o- ; public clamour and a useless expenditure of lives and ammunition, is not the surest road to ensure triumph, or gain ascr.be to their own neglect all losses result- j respect foi 'heir military capacities. þÿ This eons:., at þÿ marching up the bib, and no other advantage than moistening ll then marching down þÿagain, with ground with the blood of good soldiers, is a sorry way ot promoting the Gernu n cause, the interests of Holstein, and the reputation of the troops. OPENING OF THE DANISH CHAM- BERS. The Danish Chamber was opened on the 5th by Royal Commission : l be President of the Ministry read ihe following address : þÿ þÿ After the lapse of only a few months we greet you again, and welcome you to the resumption of your exertions for the welfare of the country. The short interval has been marked by events important liolh for us and our people. þÿ Immediately alter the termination of the former Diet we succeeded in concluding, by the mediation of Great Britain, a peace with Prussia in the name of the Germanic Confederation. The conduct which our Government was by the terms of the peace bound to observe towards Germany lias been conscientiously maintained, and as in our policy we have always pursued the course recommended by the Powers in friendly relations with us, and especially the mediating State, in the same manner those Powers have exhibited their interest in the welfare ofGermany, as they have, with us, signed the protocol accepted in London on the 2d of August, and which afterwards received also the assent of Austria. þÿ So much the more have we reason
ofGermany has not, only deferred the ratification of the treaty of peace far beyond the term assigned, hot still places

obstacles in the way of that ratification being completed. þÿ In consequence of this lamentable condition of affairs the conclusion of the peace has been without influence on events in Holstein, as conditions of the treaty referring to ihe intervention of the Bund, in order to restore legal y and order in this Duchy, at the same time prevented us from obtaining the same object by the employment of the power at our own command. þÿ The circumstances of Germany have also contributed to render of no effect the Royal message we addressed to our misguided subjects, containing our Royal promise to agree to summon a body of men elected from the different parts of the monarchy for the temporary settlement of the points in dispute. þÿ After this attempt, answered by a hostile challenge, nothing remained but to meet revolt by arms. God was with us. Our army, received joyfully by the faithful population of Schleswig, has, with heroic courage, opened a hloodv path, as far as it was permitted to advance, and stands again victorious on the þÿ wall of þÿDenmark. þÿ With the restoration of the legal authority in Schleswig, the necessity of regulating the disturbed commercial relations between the Duchies and the Monarchy became very evident. In reference to them, and the necessity of proceeded knitting together, as firmly as possible, the hand of connection between both these portions of the State, that had been loosened by the continuance of the war, we have, by a provisional law, according to paragraph 30 of the Con-

stitution, equalized the customs dues, and abolished the customs frontier bcj iween Denmark and Schleswig, and in connection with this measure shall, it necessary, abolish the odrui in all thu towns of the State, with the exception of Copenhagen. We feel so much the more confidence that this measure will have the consent of the Diet, as it lias been for a long time generally desired, and t he subject of preparatory negotiations. þÿ The financial resources of the State, notwithstanding t lie continuance of the war, are not exhausted, and it is hoped the revenue of the running half of the financial year will be sufficient to cover the expenditure, without resorting to the power conferred by the law, authorising the levy of a war tax, passed on the loth of May last, to issue credit notes to the amount of 2,000,001) rix dollars ; so that the ordinary and extraordinary revenue of the next financial year can lie applied exclusively to cover the necessary expenditure. þÿ W e know, and we rejoice to lie able to declare it among you, that the storms which have visited our country, how lamentable otherwise their effects may have been, have served to strengthen the bond between King and people, who to complain that the present condition I have had so much to hear and endure together þÿ Tlie st: g and sound spirit of the people will mi mute also the ire- ivh>
are called to decide with the Government on the welfare of the State. In that hope we wish the blessing of God on you and your þÿlabours.

From the St. Thomas Times, Nov. 20 The British screw-propeller Merlin, Captain Sampson, of 400 tons, and 120 horse power, from New York and Bermuda, arrived here on Monday at 4 þÿo clockp. m. The þÿ þÿMerlin left New York on Saturday the 9th instant, at 3 þÿo clockp. m., reached Bermuda on the following Wednesday at 11 þÿo clock a. m. She remained at Bermuda 24 hours, then steamed for this port; thus making the whole trip from New York to this port, including detention at Bermuda, in 9 days and one hour. As this is the first visit of this fine vessel to our port we would wish to make a few remarks respecting her. We are told by one of the gentlemen, who came a passenger, that she is a very fine sea boat, and that her accommodations are all that can be desired. We also learn from another source, that Mr. Cunard, the enterprising Manager of this line, and a passenger in her, attributes the length of her present passage to a want of a little better trim, <fcc., occasioned by the result of the very precipitate manner in which the arrangements of this her first voyage had to be completed. Mr. Cunard therefore, estimates her future voyages not to exceed one week, detentions included. Her first passenger list has proved an exceedingly encouraging one, having no fewer than 50 names thereon, 10 of whom were lor Bermuda. We are unable to ascertain what are the exact prospects for the return trip, but if not sufficiently encouraging it must be attributed to the fact that her coming hither, was not known For certain,

amongst the neighbouring islands, as the enquiry of several letters received here from many places bear testimony to ; the result of her success will therefore be more fully tested by the experience of T» few voyages.

By the Clyde we have received no files from Jamaica, but we are sorry to state, from what we can learn that the Cholera so far from being on the decrease, has reached a frightful extent in that island. The loss of life is very great, the accounts vary from 150 to 200 a day. W'e trust that this frightful mortality is exaggerated, though from the steadiness .t its increase since its first appearance, vc fear the intelligence is but too true. The unfortunate inhabitants arc dying so fast that it is said, Coffins cannot be prepared quickly enough to supply the demand for them ; and in some instances pits were obliged to be dug as a more expeditious means of burying the dead. As a means of precaution, gunpowder had been exploded in the vicinity of the towns, the effect of which, it was supposed would tend to purify the atmosphere- þÿ H».

A new process of making and baking bread and biscuits by steam lias been recently patented by Messrs. Lee and Robinson, of Wapping. By this process, the dour is placed in a hopper, in its descent through which it comes in contact with carbonated water, which immediately converts it into dough, in which form it issues from a cone below, and is cut oil into portions of a given size, when, being received hv an attendant buy, it is passed through other machines as it may |he required for bread or biscuits, into which form it is almost instantaneously converted. The batch of for education, religious exercises and bread or biscuits is then placed in an oven heated by the same steam machine, b\ which the whole of the machinery is worked, and within a few minutes (ten or twelve) is ready for table. This application of the powers of steam is most

ingenious, and appears likely to effect a complete revolution in the baking trade, as two or three hoys will lie capable, with one man as an overseer, to conduct the baking operations of a pretty large establishment ; while, the baneful nightwork, of which the journeymen bakers now so much complain, in watching the sponge, and preparing the þÿmorning s i .itch of bread, may he entirely superseded. (Sagged Dormitory. The first report of þÿ The London Ragged þÿDormitorj has just been published. It is an institution established under the patronage of Lord Ashley, the
a limited number of male thieves, or vagrants, from the age of sixteen to

that age, who are anxious to reform, but being destitute of friends, or a home, or their friends being worthless, and hav- : iug no provision made for them when sent from prison, arc obliged (although

« m <o AT I 3 reluctantly) again to resort to begging and stealing for a miserable existence. There is no restriction as to parish or district. Every applicant undergoes a strict investigation of his past life, and, if found to be a suitable candidate, is admitted into the receiving-room, on probation, for a fortnight, and may attend the school during school hours. He only receives one pound of bread per day during the period of his probation. At the expiration of the fortnight he is fully admitted to the benefit of the institution. Should there be any doubt of his sincerity, even after lie has completed his probation and been admitted, he will he kept on low diet another fortnight. It is, therefore, useless for any one to apply who is not truly tired of the miserable life he is leading, and also willing to w ork and make himself generally useful. The inmates are not allowed to associate or form acquaintance with loose characters in or out of the neighbourhood, neither to correspond by letter or otherw ise, without first having the sanction of the governor. Should money be given to the inmates it will he deposited in the þÿgovernor hands, s who will see that no improper use is made of it. Ouarrelling, fighting, and swearing are prohibited, and clothing is not given hut lent to the inmates. They are fully employed, hut there are times set apart

duties, and exercise. Since the institution has been established there have been 103 applications for admission ; 70 have been admitted from the streets, 13 from various prisons (recommended by the chaplains), 23 did not complete tb n probation, 4 were dismissed for misconduct, 3 absconded after completing their probation, 5 were dismissed for want of funds, 2 restored to their friends, 2 filling situations m England, 15 emigrated to Australia, 5 to the United States, ,40 at present in the institution. The report considers this as a highly successful ex periment, and requests pecuniary aid, as well as gifts of cast-off clothing and books. Ibid. þÿ
